context.concept_name: Running and iterating on a supplied stable-SDK Flutter project

coverage.learning_objective: Run one supplied stable-SDK project and verify a source change with the appropriate reload action.

required_facts.statement: Run a supplied project with `flutter run` on a physical or virtual target in debug mode to use hot reload.
After modifying a Dart source file, enter `r` in the running terminal or use the editor's hot-reload control and check the running app for the change.
Hot reload preserves application state, whereas hot restart restarts the Flutter app and loses that state.
A source change becomes visible only if the changed code executes again; use restart when the change requires application initialization to run again.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine opening a supplied mobile app, making the supplied source edit, and finding that the running screen still looks unchanged. There are two questions to separate: did you send the change to the app, and did the changed code execute again? Running and iterating means connecting an edit to an observable result on the supplied target, not merely saving the file.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Run a supplied project with `flutter run` on a physical or virtual target in debug mode to use hot reload. After modifying a Dart source file, enter `r` in the running terminal or use the editor's hot-reload control and check the running app for the change. Hot reload preserves application state, whereas hot restart restarts the Flutter app and loses that state. A source change becomes visible only if the changed code executes again; use restart when the change requires application initialization to run again.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Follow the running example through both actions. With hot reload, ask what the screen should show given that its current application state is preserved. With hot restart, ask what should show after application initialization runs again and the earlier state is lost. Those are different expected results even when both actions use the same edited source. This comparison explains why you should choose an action from the changed code's need to execute again, rather than assuming that the most convenient action proves the edit. The final evidence is the intended change in the running app, not just an action taken in the terminal.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Start the supplied project with `flutter run` on the provided physical or virtual target in debug mode. Make the exercise's Dart edit, then enter `r` in the running terminal or use the editor's hot-reload control. Compare the intended change with the running app. Suppose the exercise has already put the app into a particular state: hot reload keeps that state, so you can check the edit without treating this as a fresh application start. If the edit affects initialization that must run again, use restart and check the result after initialization instead.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Hot reload is not a promise that every edit immediately appears. A changed section must execute again. Hot restart is not state-preserving reload under another name: it restarts the Flutter app and loses its current state.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Separate the evidence you collect: the project is running in debug mode, the reload action was sent, and the expected source change is visible. If visibility is missing, ask whether the changed code has executed again before assuming that saving or reloading failed. Choose the restart action when initialization is the part that needs to run again.

video_need.reason: A running target can show an edit taking effect and the different state outcomes of reload and restart.

context.concept_name: Dart variable declarations and inferred types

coverage.learning_objective: Declare one function's values with correct inferred types and permitted reassignment.

required_facts.statement: `var name = value;` infers the variable's type from its initializer; an explicit declaration uses `Type name = value;`.
An ordinary variable can be reassigned with `name = value;`, subject to its declared or inferred type.
`final` permits a variable to be assigned once; `const` declares a compile-time constant and is implicitly final.
Use `final` for a value that will not be reassigned and `var` for a local value that must be reassigned.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied function keeps track of an order count and a fixed delivery label. The count changes as the function works, but the label should keep its first value. A declaration gives a value a name and establishes the type and reassignment rules that later statements must respect.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: `var name = value;` infers the variable's type from its initializer; an explicit declaration uses `Type name = value;`. An ordinary variable can be reassigned with `name = value;`, subject to its declared or inferred type. `final` permits a variable to be assigned once; `const` declares a compile-time constant and is implicitly final. Use `final` for a value that will not be reassigned and `var` for a local value that must be reassigned.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Trace the count declaration as a contract that continues after its first line. Its initializer establishes the inferred type, and its later assignment must remain within that type. Trace the label differently: the final modifier permits its one assignment but not a later replacement of that variable's value. For a const declaration, additionally ask whether the value is a compile-time constant. These questions let you explain the modifier choice in the supplied function: the count needs reassignment, the label does not, and a compile-time value has the additional const property. The declaration and the function's later statements should tell the same story.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: For a changing count, `var orderCount = 2;` infers a type from the integer initializer. At this point orderCount is 2. After `orderCount = 3;`, it is 3: the reassignment stays within its inferred type. `int orderCount = 2;` is the explicit-type alternative, not a second declaration to place beside the first. Contrast `final deliveryLabel = 'Ready';`: this example assigns the label once and does not reassign it; a later replacement is not permitted. A compile-time value can instead be declared with `const`. Choose the modifier according to whether this variable will receive another assignment.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: `var` does not mean that later assignments can use any type. Inference establishes a type from the initializer. Also distinguish a final variable from a compile-time constant: both restrict assignment, but only `const` makes the declaration a compile-time constant.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Read the supplied function before choosing the modifier. Identify the first value, determine whether another assignment is needed, and compare every later assigned value with the variable's type. Check a changing variable and a non-reassigned variable separately. This makes the declaration an intentional part of the function's behavior rather than a modifier chosen by habit.

video_need.reason: A short annotated pair of declarations and reassignments explains the distinction without a running demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Complete declarations and a permitted reassignment for orderCount and deliveryLabel inside a supplied function, using inferred types and choosing modifiers according to whether each value changes.
practice_anchor.success: orderCount is declared with var and initialized to 2, then reassigned to 3. deliveryLabel is declared with final and initialized to 'Ready', with no later reassignment.

context.concept_name: Interpreting Dart analyzer diagnostics

coverage.learning_objective: Correct one supplied analyzer diagnostic at its source location with clean reanalysis.

required_facts.statement: Analyzer diagnostics identify source problems with a diagnostic name, message, and source location.
Use the diagnostic's description and documented correction to edit the indicated source, then run `flutter analyze` again to check the correction.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: You edit a supplied Dart declaration and the analyzer reports a source problem. The diagnostic is a precise starting point: it has a name, a message, and a location. Correcting it means connecting that report to the indicated statement and then checking the result with analysis again.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Analyzer diagnostics identify source problems with a diagnostic name, message, and source location. Use the diagnostic's description and documented correction to edit the indicated source, then run `flutter analyze` again to check the correction.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The loop has two reports, with the source edit between them. The first report tells you what problem to investigate and where; the second tells you whether your documented correction addressed it. Keep those roles separate. For the supplied reassignment diagnostic, the useful reasoning is the connection between the message, the indicated statement, and the documented correction—not the number of lines changed. If reanalysis still reports the problem, the same three pieces of evidence remain the starting point. A clean result for that diagnostic closes this particular correction loop without requiring unrelated changes elsewhere.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the exercise supplies a diagnostic about one reassignment. Read its name and message, go to its source location, and compare the indicated declaration and assignment with the diagnostic's documented correction. Make that correction at the identified source, then run `flutter analyze`. The useful result is a new analysis report showing whether that particular problem remains. Keep the example focused on the supplied diagnostic rather than making unrelated edits elsewhere in the project.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Changing a nearby line is not itself evidence that the diagnostic is fixed. The verification step is reanalysis. Likewise, the source location identifies the reported problem; it is not an instruction to rewrite the whole surrounding file.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Use a small evidence trail: retain the original diagnostic name, note the source location you edited, and compare the new report with the original one. If the same problem remains, return to its description and correction. This teaches a repeatable diagnostic-to-source loop without introducing general debugging or editor setup as new Flutter topics.

video_need.reason: An analyzer report, source navigation, correction and clean reanalysis form a useful tool workflow.

practice_anchor.objective: Correct one supplied reassignment diagnostic at its indicated source location in supplied scaffolding, using its description and documented correction, then run `flutter analyze` again.
practice_anchor.success: The indicated source is corrected without unrelated changes, and a fresh `flutter analyze` report is clean.

context.concept_name: Dart expressions and ordinary operators

coverage.learning_objective: Implement one eligibility expression that gives the specified result for supplied inputs.

required_facts.statement: Arithmetic operators `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `~/`, and `%` mean addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, integer division, and remainder respectively.
Comparisons `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, and `>=` produce boolean results for equality, inequality, and ordering tests.
Combine boolean conditions using `&&` for conjunction, `||` for disjunction, and `!` for negation.
Operator precedence determines expression grouping; parentheses explicitly choose the grouping.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A mobile order screen needs an eligibility result from supplied values. You might need to compare a total with a limit and combine that comparison with another boolean condition. An expression describes how values are calculated or tested; its grouping matters as much as the individual operators.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Arithmetic operators `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `~/`, and `%` mean addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, integer division, and remainder respectively. Comparisons `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, and `>=` produce boolean results for equality, inequality, and ordering tests. Combine boolean conditions using `&&` for conjunction, `||` for disjunction, and `!` for negation. Operator precedence determines expression grouping; parentheses explicitly choose the grouping.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Separate the eligibility expression into questions in the same order as its intended grouping. The amount comparison asks whether the amount meets the limit. The delivery boolean supplies another true-or-false input. Conjunction requires both; disjunction represents an alternative; negation reverses a boolean condition. Before combining them, write the intended decision in plain language so an alternative is not accidentally treated as a requirement. Parentheses then record the grouping you chose. The numerical division examples are a reminder that an operator expresses a specific operation, not just a general instruction to calculate something with two values.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Take an illustrative eligibility rule: the amount is at least 20 and delivery is enabled. With `amount = 24` and `deliveryEnabled = true`, `amount >= 20 && deliveryEnabled` gives true; with amount 18 it gives false. For arithmetic, trace the same inputs through three different operations: `5 / 2 = 2.5` is division, retaining the fractional part; `5 ~/ 2 = 2` is integer division, giving the whole-number quotient; `5 % 2 = 1` is remainder, because two groups of 2 use 4 of the 5, leaving 1. The remainder is not the quotient or its fractional part. These are separate illustrative expressions. When an eligibility rule combines alternatives and requirements, parentheses record the intended grouping.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: The symbol `=` used for assignment is not the equality comparison `==`. Also, division, integer division, and remainder answer different questions. An expression can contain the right values but still produce the wrong eligibility result if its logical groups do not match the requirement.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Trace one supplied input at a time: compute the arithmetic parts, evaluate the comparisons, then combine the boolean results with the intended grouping. Include a case that should be eligible and a case that should not. State the expected result before evaluating the expression, so you are checking the requirement rather than accepting whichever result the expression happens to produce.

video_need.reason: Tracing grouped arithmetic and boolean results helps expose an eligibility expression that uses the wrong operators.

context.concept_name: Dart string interpolation

coverage.learning_objective: Build one interpolated label with the specified output for supplied model values.

required_facts.statement: Use single or double quotes to write a string literal.
Write `$identifier` to interpolate a variable or `${expression}` to interpolate a more complex expression in a string.
Interpolation obtains an object's string representation by calling its `toString()` method.
Use a backslash to escape a matching quote within a quoted string.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order card needs a label containing a supplied order number. A string literal provides the fixed text, and interpolation places the changing value inside that text without changing the label's intended wording.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Use single or double quotes to write a string literal. Write `$identifier` to interpolate a variable or `${expression}` to interpolate a more complex expression in a string. Interpolation obtains an object's string representation by calling its `toString()` method. Use a backslash to escape a matching quote within a quoted string.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: With a supplied integer variable `orderNumber` equal to 12, `'Order $orderNumber'` produces `Order 12`. If the label includes an expression rather than just a variable name, braces mark the expression: with `count` equal to 2, `'Items: ${count + 1}'` produces `Items: 3`. Use single or double quotes consistently, and escape a matching quote with a backslash when it occurs inside the literal. Interpolation uses the interpolated object's string representation; it is not a separate model-formatting rule.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: The braces in `${expression}` are significant. `$identifier` is for a variable name, not a whole arithmetic expression. Also do not assume interpolation chooses a special business display format: it obtains the object's representation through `toString()`.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the scope focused
teaching_blocks.content: Check the exact output characters against the supplied label requirement, including punctuation and spaces.

video_need.reason: Two short interpolated labels and their literal outputs are sufficient.

practice_anchor.success: The label evaluates to exactly Order 12: 3 items, 'confirmed', using variable interpolation, a braced arithmetic expression, and an escaped matching quote.

context.concept_name: Dart functions with named and optional parameters

coverage.learning_objective: Implement one function whose required, named and optional arguments bind as specified.

required_facts.statement: Define a function with typed parameters and a return type, using `return expression;` in its body to produce a result.
Required positional arguments bind in parameter order and must be supplied by the caller.
Parameters inside `{...}` are named and are passed with `parameterName: value`; mark a named parameter `required` when callers must provide it.
Parameters inside `[...]` are optional positional parameters; use `= constantValue` to supply a default when the caller omits an optional parameter.
An arrow body `=> expression;` is shorthand for returning that expression.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order calculation should produce a result from a clear set of inputs. A function packages that calculation behind parameters and a return type. The caller must know which inputs bind by position, which bind by name, and which can be omitted.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Define a function with typed parameters and a return type, using `return expression;` in its body to produce a result. Required positional arguments bind in parameter order and must be supplied by the caller. Parameters inside `{...}` are named and are passed with `parameterName: value`; mark a named parameter `required` when callers must provide it. Parameters inside `[...]` are optional positional parameters; use `= constantValue` to supply a default when the caller omits an optional parameter. An arrow body `=> expression;` is shorthand for returning that expression.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The declaration is the caller's binding contract. Look at the parameter section before following the body: positional parameters answer which argument comes first or next, named parameters answer which label identifies the argument, and defaults answer what is used if an optional argument is omitted. Then follow the bound values to the returned result. A wrong result may come from binding the right values to the wrong positional parameters rather than from arithmetic inside the function. In the named case, check the parameter name and required marker independently. These checks keep calling rules separate from the computation they feed.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: An optional parameter is not the same thing as a required named parameter. Naming improves explicit binding but does not, by itself, make the input mandatory. An arrow body returns one expression; it is not a substitute for an arbitrary multi-statement function body.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: For the supplied function, pair every call argument with its parameter and record the value that parameter receives. Include one call using all required inputs and one that omits an optional input. Follow the body to its returned expression and verify the expected result. Keep the implementation to the specified input contract rather than adding unrelated overload-like alternatives.

video_need.reason: Annotated call-to-parameter binding and returned values clarify the different argument forms.

context.concept_name: Dart classes and constructors for application models

coverage.learning_objective: Implement one application model whose constructor establishes all required fields.

required_facts.statement: Declare an instance's typed fields inside a class and access an instance member with `instance.member`.
A generative constructor has the class's name and initializes a newly created instance.
Use initializing formal parameters such as `ClassName(this.field);` or `ClassName({required this.field});` to assign arguments to instance fields.
Initialize final instance fields at declaration, with initializing formal parameters, or in an initializer list before the constructor body runs.
A `final` instance field is assigned once and cannot subsequently be reassigned.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order model needs a stable identity and a display label each time a new order instance is created. A class defines the instance fields, and its constructor establishes the required field values. This makes the constructor the place to check whether the model starts with the data its callers expect.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Declare an instance's typed fields inside a class and access an instance member with `instance.member`. A generative constructor has the class's name and initializes a newly created instance. Use initializing formal parameters such as `ClassName(this.field);` or `ClassName({required this.field});` to assign arguments to instance fields. Initialize final instance fields at declaration, with initializing formal parameters, or in an initializer list before the constructor body runs. A `final` instance field is assigned once and cannot subsequently be reassigned.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Think of the constructor as the transition from supplied arguments to an initialized instance. In the Order example, pair each argument with the final field it establishes and then read that field through the created instance. If the initializing formals are named, use their names for the pairing; if positional, use their positions. A final field's once-assigned rule remains in effect after construction. The important difference from an ordinary changing local variable is that the instance field cannot later be reassigned. Keep every required field's initialization visible rather than expecting the constructor body to repair a missing final-field initialization afterward.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Declaring a final instance field does not make its initialization optional. context.concept_name: Declarative composition with immutable widget configurations

coverage.learning_objective: Compose one small screen whose immutable widget tree matches the supplied UI structure.

required_facts.statement: Widgets are immutable descriptions of part of a user interface, with their configuration held in final fields.
Compose a widget tree by passing another widget to a `child` argument or a list of widgets to `children`, according to the receiving widget's API.
To change a widget's configuration, create a new widget configuration rather than mutate the existing widget.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied screen has a heading and a body section. In Flutter you describe that structure with widgets rather than editing an existing widget object to change what it says. Think of the widget tree as the current UI description, made from configurations passed into other widgets.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Widgets are immutable descriptions of part of a user interface, with their configuration held in final fields. Compose a widget tree by passing another widget to a `child` argument or a list of widgets to `children`, according to the receiving widget's API. To change a widget's configuration, create a new widget configuration rather than mutate the existing widget.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Read the composition from both sides of each connection. The outer widget API says whether it accepts one child or a children list; the nested configuration supplies the widget or widgets that fill that role. This is why you should not infer the argument name solely from how many visual parts you see. In the changed-heading case, the old configuration still describes its old input and the new configuration describes the changed one. That separates immutable descriptions from the ordinary fact that an interface can have different descriptions over time. First check structure, then compare the input values in each description.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: For the supplied structure, identify which receiving API expects a single `child` and which expects a list called `children`. Put the body widget into a single-child slot when that API requests one widget; use the children list when the container accepts several. Suppose the heading input changes from one supplied label to another. Create a new widget configuration containing the new value rather than assigning over a final field of the earlier widget. The composition exercise is about matching the described UI structure, not yet about how a particular layout allocates space.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Immutable does not mean the screen can never change. It means the existing widget configuration is not mutated; a changed description is represented by a new configuration. Also, `child` and `children` are receiving-API choices, not interchangeable argument spellings.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Trace the supplied tree from the outer widget to its leaves. At each connection, check whether the receiving constructor expects one child or a collection. Compare the completed description with the required heading/body structure. For a changed input, point to the new configuration that represents it and leave the old configuration unchanged.

context.concept_name: StatelessWidget build and rebuild behavior

coverage.learning_objective: Implement one stateless view that derives the specified output from current inputs.

required_facts.statement: A StatelessWidget describes UI using its configuration and the BuildContext passed to its build method.
Implement `Widget build(BuildContext context)` to return the widget subtree derived from those inputs.
The framework may call build after insertion, a configuration change, or a change to an inherited dependency; do not rely on build running only once.
The build method should have no side effects beyond building a widget.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order summary receives its current label as configuration and should describe a subtree from that input. A StatelessWidget is useful here because the teaching target is deriving UI from current configuration and context, not storing a changing local value inside the view.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: A StatelessWidget describes UI using its configuration and the BuildContext passed to its build method. Implement `Widget build(BuildContext context)` to return the widget subtree derived from those inputs. The framework may call build after insertion, a configuration change, or a change to an inherited dependency; do not rely on build running only once. The build method should have no side effects beyond building a widget.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Repeatability is the important property to check in this build method. If the configuration says Ready, the returned subtree should describe Ready. If a later configuration says Dispatched, derive the description from that later input rather than assuming the earlier build was the only one. The framework can also call build because an inherited dependency changed. Treat the supplied context as part of the input relationship, not merely a parameter that is always irrelevant. By keeping the method free of side effects beyond widget building, you avoid assigning a one-time operation to a method the framework may call repeatedly.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: In the supplied stateless view, implement `Widget build(BuildContext context)` and return the subtree described by the current inputs. Imagine receiving the label Ready first and Dispatched in a later configuration. Each build should derive the output from the configuration it receives, so the second description uses Dispatched. Keep actions such as starting an operation out of this method: the method's job is building a widget. Its context is also an input, so a relevant inherited dependency change can lead the framework to call build again.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Stateless does not mean build runs once. The framework may call it after insertion, configuration changes, or inherited-dependency changes. If the method assumes a single call, that assumption conflicts with its role as a repeatable description of the current UI.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Review the method as a mapping from inputs to subtree. Check one configuration, then a changed configuration, and ask whether both produce the required description. Check that the method does not perform side effects beyond building widgets. Leave owner-managed mutable state and asynchronous work to their own lessons rather than trying to fit them into this stateless view.

context.concept_name: Applying constraints to size widgets and resolve ordinary overflow

coverage.learning_objective: Repair one bounded overflow by tracing parent constraints and child size.

required_facts.statement: A parent passes constraints down, children pass chosen sizes up, and parents position their children.
Constraints specify minimum and maximum width and height, and a child chooses a size within those limits.
For an overflow, inspect the parent's constraints and the child's requested size to identify which dimension cannot fit.

Bound a child with `ConstrainedBox(constraints: const BoxConstraints(minWidth: 70, minHeight: 70, maxWidth: 150, maxHeight: 150), child: child)`; these are additional bounds within the parent constraints, not replacements for them: with a parent permitting that range an oversized child is limited to 150, but tight parent constraints can force a size outside the requested range.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied card overflows its available width. Before changing arbitrary widths, separate what the parent permits from what the child requests. Flutter layout passes constraints down, receives chosen sizes back, and then positions children; a child cannot treat its preferred size as the only input.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: A parent passes constraints down, children pass chosen sizes up, and parents position their children. Constraints specify minimum and maximum width and height, and a child chooses a size within those limits. For an overflow, inspect the parent's constraints and the child's requested size to identify which dimension cannot fit. Bound a child with `ConstrainedBox(constraints: const BoxConstraints(minWidth: 70, minHeight: 70, maxWidth: 150, maxHeight: 150), child: child)`; these are additional bounds within the parent constraints, not replacements for them: with a parent permitting that range an oversized child is limited to 150, but tight parent constraints can force a size outside the requested range.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Keep four measurements separate: the parent's minimum, the parent's maximum, the child's requested size, and the child's chosen size. The constraint interval determines which chosen sizes are permitted. A requested size outside that interval does not become valid just because the child wants it. The ConstrainedBox adds bounds within that relationship; it does not remove the parent's limits. This makes the two supplied parent cases genuinely different: a parent permitting the example's range allows the 150 limit, while tight parent constraints can force a size outside the added requested range. Follow the real incoming constraints before interpreting the bound.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the parent allows the range in the brief's ConstrainedBox example. The additional bounds request a minimum of 70 and maximum of 150 in each dimension, so an oversized child is limited to 150 in that setting. Now change the scenario: the parent has tight constraints that force a size outside that requested range. The ConstrainedBox bounds do not replace those parent constraints. In the overflow exercise, inspect the actual parent's minimum and maximum width and height, then compare the child's requested size. Identify the dimension that cannot fit before selecting the supplied repair.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Adding a ConstrainedBox is not permission to override the parent. The resulting size depends on the incoming constraints as well as the added bounds. Also, an overflow symptom does not tell you by itself whether width or height is the dimension causing the problem.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Draw a small parent-to-child trace with the actual constraints, the requested size, and the size the child can choose within the applicable limits. Compare the screen after the bounded repair with the requirement. Keep the explanation on this local constraint relationship rather than introducing scrolling or flex as universal solutions to every overflow.

context.concept_name: Linear layout with Row and Column

coverage.learning_objective: Compose one screen section with the specified main-axis and cross-axis placement.

required_facts.statement: Row arranges its children horizontally; Column arranges its children vertically.
Set `mainAxisAlignment` to position children along the primary axis and `crossAxisAlignment` along the perpendicular axis.
`start`, `end`, and `center` select alignment within an axis, while main-axis `spaceBetween`, `spaceAround`, and `spaceEvenly` distribute free space.
For a Row, horizontal start depends on text direction; for a Column, vertical start depends on vertical direction.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied order section needs its label and amount placed along a horizontal line, while another section stacks fields vertically. Row and Column choose the primary direction; alignment then positions children along that direction and across it.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Row arranges its children horizontally; Column arranges its children vertically. Set `mainAxisAlignment` to position children along the primary axis and `crossAxisAlignment` along the perpendicular axis. `start`, `end`, and `center` select alignment within an axis, while main-axis `spaceBetween`, `spaceAround`, and `spaceEvenly` distribute free space. For a Row, horizontal start depends on text direction; for a Column, vertical start depends on vertical direction.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: For a Row, reason about horizontal placement as main-axis placement and vertical placement as cross-axis placement. For a Column, swap those roles. If the requirement is equal gaps between neighboring items, compare it with main-axis `spaceBetween`; if it calls for spacing around items or evenly distributed gaps, compare `spaceAround` and `spaceEvenly`. Use start, end, or center when the intended placement is alignment rather than free-space distribution. Interpret a Row's horizontal start using text direction and a Column's vertical start using vertical direction.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Main axis does not always mean horizontal. It is horizontal for Row and vertical for Column. Start is also not an unconditional synonym for left or top; the relevant direction determines it.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the scope focused
teaching_blocks.content: Sketch the required arrangement and label both axes before choosing the properties.

In this example, that vertical alignment uses the Row’s height, established by its tallest child, rather than the full screen height.

context.concept_name: Declaring and loading bundled application assets

coverage.learning_objective: Declare and load one supplied image using the correct bundle key.

required_facts.statement: Declare bundled asset paths under `flutter: assets:` in pubspec.yaml, preserving the required YAML indentation.
An asset's path relative to pubspec.yaml provides its logical key in the asset bundle.
Load a declared bundled image with `Image.asset('assetKey')`; the key must match the declared resource.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied order screen includes an image shipped with the application. Loading it requires agreement between the asset declaration and the key used in the widget, not merely the presence of an image file somewhere in the project.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content:
Declare bundled asset paths in pubspec.yaml under the `flutter` section's `assets` list. For an illustrative resource at `assets/order.png` relative to pubspec.yaml, use:
```yaml
flutter:
  assets:
    - assets/order.png
```
`assets:` is indented two spaces beneath `flutter:`, and the asset entry is indented beneath `assets:`. The relative path supplies the logical asset-bundle key. Load the matching resource with `Image.asset('assets/order.png')`; the key must match the declaration.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Use the indented declaration above for the illustrative `assets/order.png` resource. The path relative to pubspec.yaml is its logical bundle key, so `Image.asset('assets/order.png')` refers to that same key. Compare the strings directly when the image is not the expected one. This example concerns a bundled resource, not a network image source.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: The logical key must match the declared resource. A similar filename or a path copied from a different directory is not the same key, and malformed YAML indentation is not equivalent to a valid assets declaration.

context.concept_name: Inspecting widget structure with Flutter DevTools

coverage.learning_objective: Locate the widget responsible for one supplied visual symptom using the inspector.

required_facts.statement: Open DevTools' Flutter Inspector while the application runs to inspect its live widget tree.
Enable Select Widget Mode and select the affected area in the running app to locate its widget in the tree.
Inspect the selected widget's properties and layout information, and use its source link to connect the visual symptom to application code.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied screen has a visibly misplaced control, but the source contains several similar-looking widgets. The Flutter Inspector connects the running area you select with a node in the live widget tree, its properties, and its source location.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Open DevTools' Flutter Inspector while the application runs to inspect its live widget tree. Enable Select Widget Mode and select the affected area in the running app to locate its widget in the tree. Inspect the selected widget's properties and layout information, and use its source link to connect the visual symptom to application code.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The same control can be described in three useful ways: the visible area you select, its live widget-tree node, and the application source reached through the node's link. The Inspector joins those descriptions. Use the visible selection to avoid confusing similar source widgets, then use properties and layout information to explain the supplied symptom. Finally connect that explanation to the actual source location. None of these observations should be substituted for another: a source name alone does not establish which live widget you selected, and a screenshot alone does not expose the selected widget's properties or source link.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Run the app and open DevTools' Flutter Inspector. Enable Select Widget Mode, then select the affected control in the running screen. Use the selected node to inspect its properties and layout information rather than guessing from a similarly named source widget. Follow its source link to connect the visual symptom to the application code. For the exercise, retain the selected node and the layout observation that explains why this is the relevant area to inspect.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: The Inspector's live tree is not a replacement for checking source. Its value is the connection between the selected visible area, the corresponding widget information, and the source link. Selecting the wrong area can lead you to inspect a perfectly valid but unrelated widget.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Work from symptom to node to source. Confirm that the selected node corresponds to the supplied affected area before interpreting its properties. Keep this investigation local to the UI and layout information the Inspector shows; avoid turning it into an unrelated performance or memory investigation.

context.concept_name: Dart conditional control flow

coverage.learning_objective: Implement one input-dependent decision that selects the required branch for given inputs.

required_facts.statement: Use `if (booleanCondition) { ... }` to execute a block when its condition is true.
Use `else` for the alternative branch and `else if` to test another condition when previous conditions were false.
A condition must have type bool; values of other types are not implicitly treated as true or false.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order feature has two different outcomes depending on a boolean eligibility result. A conditional chooses which block executes. It should follow the supplied decision rule rather than rely on an informal idea that a number or string counts as true.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Use `if (booleanCondition) { ... }` to execute a block when its condition is true. Use `else` for the alternative branch and `else if` to test another condition when previous conditions were false. A condition must have type bool; values of other types are not implicitly treated as true or false.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: For an if/else-if chain, keep a record of which preceding conditions were false. That is what makes a later condition eligible to be tested. In the basic two-outcome example, true takes the if block and false takes the alternative. In a longer supplied chain, do not reason as though every condition is a separate independent if statement. The chain's ordering is part of its behavior. Once you have traced the matching branch, compare only its specified outcome with the input requirement. A bool condition is required at each test point, whether the bool comes from a supplied variable or an allowed comparison.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Dart does not implicitly treat a non-bool value as true or false. A count or label must not be used directly as the condition just because another language or an informal rule would treat it as truthy.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Make a small input-to-branch table. Mark each earlier condition true or false, identify the branch that executes, and compare its outcome with the requirement. Include a case for the alternative branch. This is a decision-tracing exercise, not an invitation to add more cases than the supplied feature requires.

context.concept_name: Null-safe Dart types and nullable-value handling

coverage.learning_objective: Repair one nullable-value use with an explicit guard or fallback and no unjustified non-null assertion.

required_facts.statement: Append `?` to a type to allow null; an ordinary non-nullable type excludes null.
Guard a local nullable variable with a null check before using it as non-null, allowing flow analysis to promote it where applicable.
Use `value ?? fallback` to substitute a fallback when the value is null.
Use `?.` to access a member only when the receiver is not null.
The postfix `!` asserts that a value is not null; if it is null the assertion fails at runtime, so handle an uncertain nullable value with a check instead.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied order model may have no delivery note. Nullable typing makes that absence explicit: the code should handle a missing value before using it as present. The goal is not to silence a type warning, but to choose the behavior the feature requires when the value is absent.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Append `?` to a type to allow null; an ordinary non-nullable type excludes null. Guard a local nullable variable with a null check before using it as non-null, allowing flow analysis to promote it where applicable. Use `value ?? fallback` to substitute a fallback when the value is null. Use `?.` to access a member only when the receiver is not null. The postfix `!` asserts that a value is not null; if it is null the assertion fails at runtime, so handle an uncertain nullable value with a check instead.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Follow the absent note without pretending it is a present string. The nullable type allows that absence; the chosen null-handling operation determines the next behavior. A check can establish presence for a local value where promotion applies, a fallback chooses another value for null, and conditional access avoids a member access when the receiver is null. An assertion instead claims that null is impossible at that point. These are different claims about the same input. In the supplied present and absent cases, state which claim is justified before choosing the operator, rather than treating all null-related operators as interchangeable conveniences.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative local `String? note`, use a null check before treating it as non-null where flow analysis can promote it. If the required absent-note label is No note, `note ?? 'No note'` supplies that fallback only when note is null. A member access with `?.` runs only for a non-null receiver. Compare a present note with a null note: the first retains its text, while the second uses the specified absence behavior. Do not insert `!` simply because the present-note case worked.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: The postfix `!` is an assertion, not a check or a fallback. If the asserted value is null, the assertion fails at runtime. Also, promotion from a null check is subject to flow analysis; the brief does not promise that every nullable expression is promoted in every context.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Trace both possible states of the local value. Identify which operation checks presence, which supplies a fallback, and which accesses a member conditionally. Use an assertion only when its non-null claim is actually justified; for uncertain data, keep the explicit check. Leave nullable route parameters and service responses to their later application lessons.

video_need.reason: Present and absent input traces make null checks, fallback and assertion distinct.

Adding `?? 0` supplies zero when that result is null, satisfying the function’s non-nullable return type.

context.concept_name: Using typed Dart collections and generic type arguments

coverage.learning_objective: Construct and access one typed model collection while rejecting incompatible element types.

required_facts.statement: A `List<T>` is an ordered collection with elements constrained to T; create a typed literal with `<T>[...]` and access elements using zero-based indexing.
A `Set<T>` stores unique elements; create one with `<T>{...}` and add elements using `add`.
A `Map<K, V>` associates unique keys with values; create `<K, V>{key: value}`, write with `map[key] = value`, and read with `map[key]`.
A map lookup can return null when its key is absent, even when its value type is non-nullable.
Adding an incompatible type to a typed collection is an error rather than an automatic conversion to the element type.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order feature needs an ordered sequence of items, a collection of unique tags, and values found by an identity key. List, Set, and Map provide different collection relationships, with type arguments describing the elements or key/value pairs each accepts.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: A `List<T>` is an ordered collection with elements constrained to T; create a typed literal with `<T>[...]` and access elements using zero-based indexing. A `Set<T>` stores unique elements; create one with `<T>{...}` and add elements using `add`. A `Map<K, V>` associates unique keys with values; create `<K, V>{key: value}`, write with `map[key] = value`, and read with `map[key]`. A map lookup can return null when its key is absent, even when its value type is non-nullable. Adding an incompatible type to a typed collection is an error rather than an automatic conversion to the element type.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Trace each collection using the relationship it promises. The list's first and second items have indexes 0 and 1, so an index is a position rather than an arbitrary key. The set's repeated tag is still a unique element, so it does not behave as a tally of every addition. The map associates a key with a value; a missing key can yield null even though stored values have a non-nullable declared type. In each case, the type arguments constrain what can be inserted. Keep those relationship and type questions separate when checking which supplied operations are valid.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: An illustrative `<String>['Tea', 'Bread']` list has Tea at index 0 and Bread at index 1. A `<String>{'urgent'}` set models unique tags; adding the same tag does not make it a collection of repeated tag entries. A `<String, int>{'tea': 2}` map associates the tea key with a count. Read it through the key and handle a missing key with a null check or the intended fallback. These examples represent separate data needs, not three interchangeable ways to model the same behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A map whose value type is non-nullable can still return null for an absent key. Also, a typed collection does not automatically convert an incompatible value into the declared element type. Decide which collection relationship is needed before choosing its literal syntax.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: For each supplied operation, say whether order, uniqueness, or key association matters. Trace a list read, a repeated set addition, and a missing map lookup. Check that each inserted value fits the declared type and that absence is handled deliberately. This establishes the collection contract before iteration or callback-based processing is introduced.

context.concept_name: Dart iteration over application data

coverage.learning_objective: Transform one supplied collection with a loop that produces the required accumulated result.

required_facts.statement: Use `for (var element in collection) { ... }` to process collection elements.
Declare an accumulator before the loop and update it in the loop body to build a result from the elements.
A conventional loop `for (initialization; condition; update) { ... }` repeats while its condition is true, performing the update after each iteration.
`break` stops a loop and `continue` skips the remainder of the current iteration.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied list contains order quantities, and the feature needs their total. A loop processes repeated elements; an accumulator preserves the result built so far. Keeping these roles separate makes it easier to see whether each quantity contributes once.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Use `for (var element in collection) { ... }` to process collection elements. Declare an accumulator before the loop and update it in the loop body to build a result from the elements. A conventional loop `for (initialization; condition; update) { ... }` repeats while its condition is true, performing the update after each iteration. `break` stops a loop and `continue` skips the remainder of the current iteration.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: In the quantity-total example, the accumulator after one iteration becomes the starting result for the next. Write that connection explicitly: start at 0, contribute 2, carry 2 forward, contribute 3, carry 5 forward, then contribute 1. The final 6 depends on retaining the earlier contributions. If a supplied rule uses continue, record what contribution or later body statement is skipped on that iteration. If it uses break, record that there are no later iterations. For a conventional loop, also record the update after each completed iteration so the condition's next evaluation uses the intended value.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Break and continue are not two spellings of the same action. One stops the loop; the other skips the rest of the current iteration. Likewise, the accumulator belongs before the loop when it is meant to retain contributions across iterations.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Trace the current element and accumulated result together for each pass. If the exercise includes a skip or stop rule, record exactly which part of the body is bypassed and whether another iteration occurs. Compare the final result with a hand calculation on the supplied collection before generalizing to a larger collection.

context.concept_name: Dart closures and callback scope

coverage.learning_objective: Wire one callback so it uses the intended captured value when invoked.

required_facts.statement: A closure retains access to variables in the lexical scope where it was created.
Pass a function value as a callback rather than calling it immediately with parentheses.
Write an anonymous function with `(parameters) { ... }` or `(parameters) => expression` to use captured values when the callback is invoked.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied action needs a function to run later, using a value available where the callback is created. A closure retains access to that lexical scope. Passing the function and calling the function are different operations, and the timing distinction is central to this exercise.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: A closure retains access to variables in the lexical scope where it was created. Pass a function value as a callback rather than calling it immediately with parentheses. Write an anonymous function with `(parameters) { ... }` or `(parameters) => expression` to use captured values when the callback is invoked.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: A callback has both a definition site and an invocation site. At definition, its body can refer to variables from its enclosing lexical scope. At passing, the receiving API gets the function value. At invocation, the body uses that retained scope access. Keeping those three moments visible explains why an immediate function call is a different argument expression: it runs the body instead of handing over the function value for the receiver to invoke. The anonymous block and arrow forms are alternate ways to write the callback, not promises about asynchronous timing or copied snapshots of captured variables.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A callback parameter expects a function value, not automatically the result of calling the function. Also, retaining access to a lexical variable is not a claim that every captured value has been copied into a permanent snapshot at creation time.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: In the supplied example, identify the variable used from the enclosing scope, the function value passed to the receiver, and the place where the receiver invokes it. Keep the explanation on those three relationships. Do not introduce asynchronous completion merely because the action is deferred; callbacks are the topic here, not a promise of a particular scheduling mechanism.

context.concept_name: Widget configuration versus element identity

coverage.learning_objective: Demonstrate when one supplied tree update reuses an element and when it replaces it.

required_facts.statement: The framework can update an existing element with a new widget when their runtimeType and key are equal.
Changing the widget type or key prevents that element from being updated with the new widget.
Different configuration values alone do not prevent reuse when type and key still match.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A screen is rebuilt with a new widget description. To understand whether an existing element can be updated, compare widget type and key rather than just the labels in its configuration. Element identity is about the framework matching an existing element to a new description.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: The framework can update an existing element with a new widget when their runtimeType and key are equal. Changing the widget type or key prevents that element from being updated with the new widget. Different configuration values alone do not prevent reuse when type and key still match.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: In the type-and-key comparison, mark configuration as a separate concern. A label change updates what the description says, while equal runtimeType and key allow the existing element to receive that new description. If the type or key changes, the stated update condition no longer holds even if the label looks identical. This prevents reasoning backward from a visual similarity to element identity. context.concept_name: StatefulWidget and State lifecycle

coverage.learning_objective: Place one State-owned resource's initialization, configuration rebinding when needed, and disposal at the correct lifecycle boundaries, not in repeated build calls.

required_facts.statement: A State instance can persist across multiple build calls and owns its state for that lifetime.
Override initState, call `super.initState()`, and initialize owner-lifetime resources there rather than repeatedly in build.
When an update changes a configuration-dependent resource, use didUpdateWidget to detach from the old resource and bind to the new one.
Override dispose to release owned resources and call `super.dispose()` when the framework permanently removes the State.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied stateful section owns a resource that must survive ordinary rebuilds but must be released when its owner ends. State lifetime is the frame for that resource: a State instance can persist through several build calls, so resource management must not be tied to every build.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: A State instance can persist across multiple build calls and owns its state for that lifetime. Override initState, call `super.initState()`, and initialize owner-lifetime resources there rather than repeatedly in build. When an update changes a configuration-dependent resource, use didUpdateWidget to detach from the old resource and bind to the new one. Override dispose to release owned resources and call `super.dispose()` when the framework permanently removes the State.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Use the State instance as the owner-lifetime line through the example. Several builds can happen along that line without starting a new State lifetime. Initialization belongs at the start of that ownership; a configuration-dependent replacement belongs at the update that changes the resource; disposal belongs at permanent removal. The resource's binding can change while the State continues to exist. This is why a build count is not a reliable resource-creation count. For the supplied replacement, identify the old binding that must be detached and the new one that must be established, then identify the remaining resource to release at the end.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Initialize an owner-lifetime resource in `initState` and call `super.initState()`. If a later widget configuration changes which resource the section depends on, use `didUpdateWidget` to detach from the old resource and bind to the new one. Finally, when the framework permanently removes the State, release the owned resource in `dispose` and call `super.dispose()`. Trace one supplied resource through these three situations: first ownership, configuration-dependent replacement, and end of ownership.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Repeated build calls do not imply a new owner-lifetime resource should be created each time. Also, permanent removal and a configuration update are different lifecycle events: the latter may require rebinding a resource while the State continues to exist.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: For the supplied State, identify what it owns, where that ownership starts, what configuration change would replace the resource, and where ownership ends. Check that the old binding is detached before adopting its replacement. Keep actual subscription APIs for the stream lesson; here the essential skill is assigning each resource action to the correct lifecycle responsibility.

context.concept_name: Local UI updates with setState

coverage.learning_objective: Implement one local toggle whose next build reflects the changed value.

required_facts.statement: Change local State fields within `setState(() { ... });` so the framework schedules a build reflecting the changed state.
The setState callback runs synchronously and must not be async.
Changing a field without setState might not schedule a build and might leave the displayed UI unchanged.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied order section has a local count that should change when an action occurs. Updating the stored field and scheduling a UI rebuild are related but distinct. setState connects a synchronous local mutation with a framework build that can describe the new value.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Change local State fields within `setState(() { ... });` so the framework schedules a build reflecting the changed state. The setState callback runs synchronously and must not be async. Changing a field without setState might not schedule a build and might leave the displayed UI unchanged.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The supplied count has two observations: its stored field value and the UI derived from it. The setState callback changes the first synchronously, and the scheduled build reflects that change in the second. This distinction explains why merely observing a changed field is not the whole UI verification. Likewise, scheduling a build without making the intended field change would not establish the specified new count. Keep the callback itself synchronous and limited to the local mutation. The completion of an asynchronous operation, when later taught, can be outside that callback rather than changing this synchronous contract.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the local count is 1 and the supplied action changes it to 2. Put that field change inside `setState(() { ... });`. The callback performs the mutation synchronously, and the framework schedules a build reflecting the changed State. Compare this with merely assigning the field: the value might change in memory without a scheduled build, leaving the displayed count unchanged. The exercise should verify the displayed outcome as well as the new field value.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A setState callback must not be async. It is the synchronous mutation boundary, not a place to await an operation. Also, the brief says an assignment without setState might leave the UI unchanged; it does not claim that such a field could never appear in a later independently triggered build.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Trace the interaction, the field before and after the synchronous callback, and the output derived on the subsequent build. Keep the local update in the owning State rather than introducing shared state. Ask whether the displayed value now agrees with the stored field, because that agreement is the purpose of this particular UI update exercise.

context.concept_name: Extracting reusable parameterized widgets

coverage.learning_objective: Extract one repeated UI section with parameters that preserve its specified behavior.

required_facts.statement: Extract a repeated UI responsibility into a dedicated widget rather than a helper method that returns widgets.
Expose differing inputs as final constructor parameters and use those parameters in build to preserve the extracted section's behavior.
Pass a callback parameter for an action the extracted section delegates to its caller.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Two supplied screen sections repeat the same UI responsibility but use different labels and actions. Extracting a dedicated widget should preserve what each section displays and delegates, while making the varying inputs explicit in its constructor.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Extract a repeated UI responsibility into a dedicated widget rather than a helper method that returns widgets. Expose differing inputs as final constructor parameters and use those parameters in build to preserve the extracted section's behavior. Pass a callback parameter for an action the extracted section delegates to its caller.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The extracted widget has an input boundary and an action boundary. Final constructor values describe the differences between the two instances, while the callback says which action the instance delegates. Follow the original label into the extracted input and the original delegated action into the callback. Those two traces provide a direct preservation check without relying on the fact that the code now has fewer repeated lines. A dedicated widget is the requested extraction unit. Keep its responsibility the same size as the repeated section, and keep caller-specific work at the caller rather than hiding it in the shared child.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine an order-action section repeated for two supplied orders. Give the extracted widget final constructor parameters for the differing labels and use them in build. Give it a callback parameter for the action it delegates to the caller. Each caller provides its own configuration and callback, so the extracted section can retain the required display and action behavior without implementing the caller's responsibility itself. Compare the original section with one extracted instance before replacing every repetition.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A helper method returning widgets is not the dedicated-widget extraction requested here. Also, extraction is not permission to move a caller-owned action into the child. The callback preserves the delegation boundary while the final parameters preserve the differing configuration.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: List what is identical across the repeated sections and what varies. Put the varying display values in constructor inputs and the delegated action in a callback input. Verify one original/extracted pair with the same inputs and observable action. Keep the extraction bounded to the repeated responsibility instead of redesigning the surrounding screen.

context.concept_name: Form validation and submission behavior

coverage.learning_objective: Implement one form gate that rejects invalid input and submits valid input once.

required_facts.statement: Create a Form with a stable `GlobalKey<FormState>` and place TextFormFields inside it.
A TextFormField validator returns an error string for invalid input and null for valid input.
Call the form state's `validate()` from the submit handler; it runs field validators and returns true only if no field reports an error.
Place the submission action inside the successful-validation branch so an invalid form does not submit and one handler invocation performs one submission.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied checkout form must reject invalid input before the submission action runs. A Form groups the fields for validation, while the submit handler uses the validation result to decide whether submission is allowed on that invocation.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Create a Form with a stable `GlobalKey<FormState>` and place TextFormFields inside it. A TextFormField validator returns an error string for invalid input and null for valid input. Call the form state's `validate()` from the submit handler; it runs field validators and returns true only if no field reports an error. Place the submission action inside the successful-validation branch so an invalid form does not submit and one handler invocation performs one submission.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Follow the invalid input all the way to the action boundary. Its validator returns an error string; validate combines the field results and returns false if a field reports an error; the submission branch must therefore not execute. Follow the corrected input through the same path: validators return null, the overall result is true when no field reports an error, and the one handler invocation enters its single submission branch. This ordering explains both checks the exercise requires: invalid input does not submit, and valid handling does not duplicate submission within the same invocation. The stable key provides access to the intended Form state.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Use a stable `GlobalKey<FormState>` for the Form and place the supplied TextFormFields inside it. A validator returns an error string for an invalid field and null when that field is valid. From the submit handler, call the form state's `validate()`. If any field reports an error, do not submit. If validation succeeds, run the submission action inside that successful branch. For an illustrative invalid delivery note, expect an error and no submission; after correcting it to the supplied valid value, one handler invocation should perform one submission.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A validator's null result means valid input, not a missing error that should be treated as failure. Also, merely calling validate does not guard an action placed outside the successful branch; the branch placement is what prevents invalid submission.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Check the form with one invalid and one valid supplied input. Record the validator result, the overall validate result, and whether the submit action occurs. Preserve the key across the form's intended use. Keep the handler to one submission in its success branch, rather than calling the same action both inside and after the branch.

context.concept_name: Flexible space allocation in linear layouts

coverage.learning_objective: Repair one linear layout so remaining space is allocated to the intended flexible children.

required_facts.statement: Row and Column can allocate remaining main-axis space to flexible children using flex factors.
Wrap a child in Expanded to require it to fill its allocated space; wrap it in Flexible with the default loose fit to allow it to be smaller.
Set each child's `flex` to specify its proportion of remaining space relative to the other flexible children.
Flex allocation requires bounded space along the main axis; an unbounded main-axis constraint cannot supply a finite remaining space.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied horizontal section has two children that must share the remaining width. Flex allocation describes that share; Expanded and Flexible then differ in whether a child must fill its allocated part or may be smaller.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Row and Column can allocate remaining main-axis space to flexible children using flex factors. Wrap a child in Expanded to require it to fill its allocated space; wrap it in Flexible with the default loose fit to allow it to be smaller. Set each child's `flex` to specify its proportion of remaining space relative to the other flexible children. Flex allocation requires bounded space along the main axis; an unbounded main-axis constraint cannot supply a finite remaining space.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Treat allocated space and chosen child size as two measurements. The 1:2 factors divide the illustrative 300 units into 100 and 200 allocated units; Expanded then requires filling the assigned share, while loose Flexible permits a smaller child. A proportion alone does not describe that fit decision. Also, the 300-unit value is remaining main-axis space, not a claim about every device or the entire screen width. Before using the ratio, establish that this remaining space is finite under the parent's constraints. If that starting point is unbounded, the proportional arithmetic cannot supply the missing finite allocation.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a bounded Row with 300 units of remaining main-axis space and two flexible children with flex factors 1 and 2. Their proportional allocations are 100 and 200. An Expanded child must fill its allocated portion. A Flexible child using the default loose fit may choose a smaller size within its allocation. These numbers are illustrative remaining-space values, not fixed screen widths. If the main axis is unbounded, there is no finite remaining space from which to make that allocation.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Flexible is not simply a differently named Expanded: the default fit is loose rather than a requirement to fill. Also, a flex ratio does not create a finite amount of remaining space when the parent provides an unbounded main axis.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Identify the primary axis, establish that it is bounded, and separate already-used space from the remaining space considered in the exercise. Compare the flex factors and the intended fit of each child. Verify the supplied layout after the change rather than assuming proportional factors alone guarantee the required appearance.
