coverage.learning_objective: Render one dynamic collection so all content remains reachable within a bounded viewport.

required_facts.statement: A ListView scrolls a linear collection within a viewport so content beyond its visible area can be reached.
For a dynamic collection, use `ListView.builder(itemCount: ..., itemBuilder: ...)` to build children on demand by index.
Give a scrolling list a bounded viewport, using a constrained parent or Expanded within a bounded Column where appropriate.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied order collection is longer than the visible screen section. A scrolling list gives it a viewport: the user can reach content outside the currently visible area. The viewport still needs bounded space from its surrounding layout.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: A ListView scrolls a linear collection within a viewport so content beyond its visible area can be reached. For a dynamic collection, use `ListView.builder(itemCount: ..., itemBuilder: ...)` to build children on demand by index. Give a scrolling list a bounded viewport, using a constrained parent or Expanded within a bounded Column where appropriate.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The list's content and its viewport answer different size questions. The content can include more orders than are visible; the viewport is the bounded area through which the user reaches them. ListView.builder describes how dynamic children are built by index on demand. Its itemCount must describe the supplied collection, and each builder index must address the intended item. When the list is placed in a Column, the bounded-parent condition remains important for the Expanded arrangement in the brief. Check that relationship before interpreting the ability to scroll as proof the surrounding layout has the required viewport bounds.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: For a dynamic supplied collection, use `ListView.builder(itemCount: ..., itemBuilder: ...)` so children are built on demand by index. The item count comes from that collection, and the builder uses the provided index for the relevant item. Give the list a bounded viewport through the supplied constrained parent, or through Expanded inside a bounded Column where appropriate. Verify an item beyond the initial visible area can be reached by scrolling, rather than checking only the first visible items.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A scrollable list is not automatically an answer to an unbounded viewport. Scrolling concerns content beyond the visible area, while the viewport itself needs bounds. Also, builder construction is on demand; this is not a requirement to create every dynamic child before anything is displayed.

context.concept_name: Adapting layouts to available screen space

coverage.learning_objective: Adapt one supplied screen so its layout meets requirements on both sides of a width breakpoint.

required_facts.statement: Use `LayoutBuilder(builder: (context, constraints) { ... })` when a layout decision depends on the space available to that subtree.
Use `MediaQuery.sizeOf(context)` for the app window's size rather than a local widget's available size.
Compare `constraints.maxWidth` with the required breakpoint and return the appropriate widget layout from an if/else branch.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied order section should change layout when its own available width crosses a breakpoint. The app window width and the width available to this particular subtree may differ, so choose the measurement that the decision actually depends on.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Use `LayoutBuilder(builder: (context, constraints) { ... })` when a layout decision depends on the space available to that subtree. Use `MediaQuery.sizeOf(context)` for the app window's size rather than a local widget's available size. Compare `constraints.maxWidth` with the required breakpoint and return the appropriate widget layout from an if/else branch.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The narrow and wide traces should use the width named by the requirement. If the subtree has 500 available units inside a larger window, the local decision uses 500, not the window's width. LayoutBuilder supplies the local constraints for that question; MediaQuery.sizeOf supplies the app window's size for a different question. Once the measurement is chosen, the comparison establishes which layout branch to return. Keep the equality case visible in the supplied breakpoint rule. A test that happens to make local and window widths equal cannot by itself demonstrate that the correct source was chosen for a locally constrained section.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Use LayoutBuilder when the required decision concerns the subtree's available space. With an illustrative breakpoint of 600 and local `constraints.maxWidth` of 500, take the supplied narrow branch; at 700, take the supplied wide branch. Write the if/else comparison to match the stated threshold rule. If the requirement instead concerns the app window, use `MediaQuery.sizeOf(context)`. These are distinct measurement questions even when the two widths happen to be equal in one test setup.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: MediaQuery's window size is not a universal substitute for local available width. A layout can be inside a narrower section of a larger window. Also, a breakpoint name alone does not define which side includes equality; the supplied comparison rule must make that explicit.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Test values on both sides of the required breakpoint and at the boundary under the supplied rule. Record the local available width when the local layout is the subject. Keep the returned layouts to the supplied alternatives rather than adding device-brand or platform checks unrelated to the available-space decision.

context.concept_name: Supporting enlarged text without losing usability

coverage.learning_objective: Repair one screen so required content remains usable at the supplied enlarged text scale.

required_facts.statement: Flutter text widgets respect the operating system's font-size setting, which changes the space required by text.
Provide layout space for enlarged text; use `Flexible(child: Text(...))` in a bounded Row when text must fit the available width rather than overflow it.
Test the screen on a small target with the largest font setting and adjust its layout so required content remains accessible.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order label fits on the supplied small screen at the ordinary font setting but becomes too large when the user enlarges text. Font-size settings change the space text needs, so the layout must be checked with enlarged text rather than treating the original fit as sufficient.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Flutter text widgets respect the operating system's font-size setting, which changes the space required by text. Provide layout space for enlarged text; use `Flexible(child: Text(...))` in a bounded Row when text must fit the available width rather than overflow it. Test the screen on a small target with the largest font setting and adjust its layout so required content remains accessible.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Use the same content in the ordinary and enlarged-text checks. The changing input is the operating system font-size setting, which changes the space text requires. If required content overflows or becomes inaccessible, the layout needs adjustment for that larger requirement. The bounded Row and Flexible pattern addresses the supplied width problem without claiming every layout is solved by one wrapper. The small-target, largest-setting check is valuable because it tests the required content under the specified demanding combination, not just a comfortable default-size layout. Record what remains accessible after the change rather than judging only whether the screen looks tidy.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: For the supplied bounded Row, use `Flexible(child: Text(...))` when the text needs to fit the available width. Then run the screen on a small target with the largest font setting. Inspect the required labels and controls, and adjust the supplied layout so required content remains accessible. This is a space-and-content check: a neat appearance at the default setting is not the same evidence as successful access with enlarged text.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A visual check at the default font size does not test the enlarged-text case. Flutter text widgets respect the operating system's font-size setting. Also, Flexible in this example belongs to a bounded Row; it is not a guarantee that every arbitrary surrounding layout has sufficient space.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Compare the same required content at the ordinary and largest settings on the small target. Identify what requires more space and whether any required content becomes inaccessible. Keep the repair focused on accommodating that content rather than disabling the user's font-size choice or replacing the supplied text with unrelated shorter labels.

context.concept_name: Preserving list-item identity with keys

coverage.learning_objective: Correct one reorderable list so each stateful item retains its identity after reordering.

required_facts.statement: A stable key combined with the same widget type lets the framework match an item's updated configuration to its element.
Set an item's `key: ValueKey(itemIdentity)` from a stable identity, not its current list position, so reordered stateful children can remain matched to the same items.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied list reorders stateful order rows. The same order should remain matched to its own row element after moving. A stable item identity gives the key a meaning that persists through a change in position.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: A stable key combined with the same widget type lets the framework match an item's updated configuration to its element. Set an item's `key: ValueKey(itemIdentity)` from a stable identity, not its current list position, so reordered stateful children can remain matched to the same items.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Use the same A and B identities in both list orders. Before reordering, each identity produces its own key. After reordering, the positions differ but those identity-derived keys still name the same items. The framework's match also includes the same widget type. This is why the comparison table needs identity, position, key, and type rather than only index and label. If a key is made from the new position instead, it names that position rather than preserving the item's identity through the move. Check the stateful row result as well as the key values under the supplied reorder fixture.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine orders A and B trading places. Give each row `key: ValueKey(itemIdentity)` using that order's stable identity. With the same widget type and the stable key, the framework can match A's updated configuration with A's element even though A now appears at a different index. If the key instead uses the current position, the position changes meaning when the list reorders. Trace item identity, key, and index in separate columns before and after the move.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A current list position is not a stable identity for an item that can move. Also, the matching condition still includes widget type; a stable key alone does not erase the requirement that the type also matches.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: For the supplied reorder, record each item's identity and key before the move and check that those values remain associated afterward. Observe the stateful rows using the exercise's expected result. Keep this lesson about matching the same items through reordering, not about generating new identities or implementing a different list data model.

media.group_title: Keeping state with reordered items

segments.label: How keys preserve stateful item identity during reordering
segments.summary: Two colored tiles illustrate why reordering widget configurations does not necessarily move their state. context.concept_name: Choosing local versus shared state ownership

coverage.learning_objective: Place one state value at the smallest owner covering all required consumers.

required_facts.statement: Keep state above the widgets that need to use it in the widget tree.
For consumers in separate branches, choose a shared ancestor as the owner rather than duplicate the same state in each branch.
Pass state down as configuration and pass callbacks down for children to request changes from the owner.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Two supplied screen branches display the same order state and can request changes to it. Duplicating that state in both branches makes ownership unclear. Put the state above its consumers and let child actions request changes from that shared owner.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Keep state above the widgets that need to use it in the widget tree. For consumers in separate branches, choose a shared ancestor as the owner rather than duplicate the same state in each branch. Pass state down as configuration and pass callbacks down for children to request changes from the owner.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Read the shared-ancestor diagram as an ownership map. The summary and action panel are consumers in separate branches, so the owner must be above both. Configuration gives each consumer the current state it needs, while callbacks give children a way to request the owner's change. That division avoids pretending the child owns the same state just because it can request a mutation. In the supplied tree, use the ancestor relation to explain why the chosen owner reaches both branches. context.concept_name: Predictable observable state mutations with ChangeNotifier

coverage.learning_objective: Implement one model mutation that exposes coherent state before notifying consumers.

required_facts.statement: A model can extend ChangeNotifier to expose state and notify listeners of changes.
Implement a mutation method that updates the model's fields before calling `notifyListeners()`.
Expose current model values through fields or getters so notified consumers can read the updated state.
Call notifyListeners when a model change might change its consumers' UI, not merely because a value was read.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied shared model changes an order value, and its listeners need to read the new value. ChangeNotifier provides the notification part of that model contract. The order of mutation and notification matters: listeners should be told after the model exposes the changed state.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: A model can extend ChangeNotifier to expose state and notify listeners of changes. Implement a mutation method that updates the model's fields before calling `notifyListeners()`. Expose current model values through fields or getters so notified consumers can read the updated state. Call notifyListeners when a model change might change its consumers' UI, not merely because a value was read.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The notification announces a model change that has already been made. In the count example, put the update to 3 before notifyListeners so a notified read sees the exposed new count. Fields or getters provide that read contract. A mere getter read is not a mutation and is not a reason to notify. The condition for notification is that a model change might change consumer UI; this retains the brief's qualification rather than requiring notification on every access. Trace the mutation and notification separately, then show the value consumers can read at the moment they receive the notification.

Keep the distinction clear

context.concept_name: Providing a shared model above its consumers

coverage.learning_objective: Place one model above its intended consumers so lookup resolves the correct instance.

required_facts.statement: Place a provider as an ancestor of all widgets that need the provided value.
A lookup using BuildContext returns the nearest matching provider of the requested type.
Use a context below the provider for lookup; a context above it cannot resolve the value that provider exposes.
A non-nullable lookup throws when there is no matching provider.
Expose the supplied existing model with `Provider<Model>.value(value: suppliedModel, child: consumerSubtree)`, where Model is its type and consumerSubtree contains the intended consumers.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied model exists, but a consumer cannot resolve it from its context. Provider lookup is a tree-scope question: the provider must be above the consumer, and the lookup context must be below the provider that exposes the value.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Place a provider as an ancestor of all widgets that need the provided value. A lookup using BuildContext returns the nearest matching provider of the requested type. Use a context below the provider for lookup; a context above it cannot resolve the value that provider exposes. A non-nullable lookup throws when there is no matching provider. Expose the supplied existing model with `Provider<Model>.value(value: suppliedModel, child: consumerSubtree)`, where Model is its type and consumerSubtree contains the intended consumers.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Provider scope is determined at the lookup context, not by the visual title of the whole screen. Start at that context and trace its ancestors for the requested type. The nearest matching provider is the value the lookup resolves. The new provider cannot serve a context above itself, even if the source code for the two is nearby. In the supplied existing-model example, Provider.value exposes that instance to the child subtree. Check both the placement of the value and the placement of each consumer's context. A missing matching non-nullable provider is a throwing lookup, not an automatically supplied empty model.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Expose the existing supplied model using `Provider<Model>.value(value: suppliedModel, child: consumerSubtree)`. Put all intended consumers inside that subtree. A lookup for Model from a context beneath this provider finds the nearest matching provider of that type. A context above this provider cannot use it. If another matching provider is nearer to a particular consumer, that nearer provider is the relevant match. Draw the lookup context beside the consumer rather than treating every context in the screen as equivalent.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Placing a provider somewhere in a file is not enough; ancestry in the widget tree is what gives lookup access. A non-nullable lookup with no matching provider throws. The nearest matching provider rule also means a lookup need not resolve a more distant provider of the same type.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Mark the provider, consumer subtree, and exact context used for the lookup. Trace upward from that context to the nearest matching type. Confirm every intended consumer is within the exposed subtree. Keep this example on an existing supplied model; ownership and automatic disposal for newly created notifiers are different provider decisions.

context.concept_name: Provider dependency ownership and disposal

coverage.learning_objective: Correct one provider declaration so its owned model is disposed once at the correct lifetime boundary.

required_facts.statement: Use `ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => Model(), child: ...)` for a newly created model that the provider owns.
ChangeNotifierProvider automatically disposes a model it creates when that provider leaves the tree.
Use `ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: existingModel, child: ...)` to expose an already-owned model rather than transfer its ownership through create.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied shared model needs a clear owner. Creating a new notifier for a provider and exposing a model already owned elsewhere are different lifetime decisions. Choose the provider constructor that matches that ownership instead of treating create and value as stylistic alternatives.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Use `ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => Model(), child: ...)` for a newly created model that the provider owns. ChangeNotifierProvider automatically disposes a model it creates when that provider leaves the tree. Use `ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: existingModel, child: ...)` to expose an already-owned model rather than transfer its ownership through create.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Begin with the model's origin. If create constructs it for this ChangeNotifierProvider, the provider owns that new model and disposes it when leaving the tree. If the supplied model already has an owner, value exposes that existing model. The constructor choice communicates a lifetime relationship rather than an incidental syntax preference. In the ownership diagram, keep the owner of the existing model visible instead of assuming that exposing it transfers creation responsibility. Use that distinction when comparing the two snippets, and do not combine them into a single pattern that treats every passed model as newly provider-owned.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: For a newly created model, use `ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => Model(), child: ...)`. That provider owns the notifier it creates and automatically disposes it when the provider leaves the tree. For an existing model supplied by another owner, use `ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: existingModel, child: ...)`. In the second case, you are exposing an already-owned instance, not transferring it through create. Trace where the model first comes from before choosing the constructor.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: An existing model should not be passed through create as though it had just been created for that provider. Automatic disposal described here applies to the model the provider creates; ownership is the distinction that selects the API.

teaching_blocks.content: A supplied view renders order data but its event handler also performs source-specific work. teaching_blocks.content: In the recommended architecture, a view renders data and forwards interaction events rather than implement business or data-source logic. The view forwards its input to the command; application logic orchestrates the action and exposes the state the view renders; source-specific work stays in the data layer. The refactor succeeds when these responsibility locations change as intended while the input and observable outcome remain the same. This is a recommended architectural division, so preserve that scope instead of calling it the only valid Flutter structure. The most useful before/after comparison is the same event and result, with the source operation no longer implemented by the view's event handler.

teaching_blocks.content: Refactor the supplied view event so it calls an existing command with the same input instead of performing the data operation itself. Compare the original handler and refactored handler by their input and observable outcome: the responsibility changes location, but the exercise does not call for changing the feature's behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: This is a recommended responsibility split, not a claim that every Flutter application has one compulsory architecture. Also, moving an operation is not enough if the view still depends directly on the concrete source API or if the refactor changes the required result.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Label each supplied statement as rendering, event forwarding, state/action orchestration, or external access. Move only the responsibility the exercise identifies and preserve the boundary's existing contract. context.concept_name: Building a widget test with supplied dependencies

coverage.learning_objective: Build one minimal test harness providing the supplied widget's required context and dependencies.

required_facts.statement: Define a widget test using `testWidgets('description', (tester) async { ... });`, which supplies a WidgetTester.
Use `await tester.pumpWidget(widget)` to build and render the widget under test.
Include the required application ancestors, such as MaterialApp for a Material screen, in the tree passed to pumpWidget.
Provide the widget's model dependencies above it in the harness so its lookups can resolve them.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied Material screen works in the app but a widget test must construct the environment it depends on. The harness is the test's widget tree, including required ancestors and model dependencies, not just the screen placed in isolation.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Define a widget test using `testWidgets('description', (tester) async { ... });`, which supplies a WidgetTester. Use `await tester.pumpWidget(widget)` to build and render the widget under test. Include the required application ancestors, such as MaterialApp for a Material screen, in the tree passed to pumpWidget. Provide the widget's model dependencies above it in the harness so its lookups can resolve them.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Compare the production screen's requirements with the harness tree, not with the entire production application. For each dependency the test screen needs, identify the ancestor or model value that the harness actually supplies. PumpWidget builds and renders that test tree; it does not implicitly borrow missing ancestors from another tree. The supplied Material screen therefore needs its relevant MaterialApp environment in the harness, and its lookups need models placed above it. Keep the initial rendering check focused on this construction. Later finder and interaction assertions will have a meaningful screen to inspect because this environment is explicit.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Define the test with `testWidgets('description', (tester) async { ... });`. Use `await tester.pumpWidget(widget)` to build and render the supplied tree. Include MaterialApp when the Material screen requires that ancestor, and place its supplied model dependencies above the screen so lookups can resolve them. Think of the harness as a deliberately smaller tree with the dependencies required for this screen, not an instruction to assume those dependencies are available because the production app provides them.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A production ancestor does not appear automatically in a separately constructed test tree. A failing lookup in a harness may reflect a missing required dependency rather than a faulty model or screen implementation. Build the required environment before judging the screen's output.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: List the screen's required ancestors and model inputs, then mark where the harness supplies each one. Pump the completed tree and verify it is the intended screen under test. Keep finder assertions and simulated interactions for the following lessons, so this first test responsibility stays focused on correct construction and rendering.

context.concept_name: Locating widgets and asserting observable UI behavior

coverage.learning_objective: Assert one observable UI result with an appropriate finder and matcher in a supplied harness.

required_facts.statement: Use `find.text('text')` to locate Text widgets displaying a given string.
Use `find.byKey(key)` for a keyed widget or `find.byType(Type)` to locate widgets of a type.
Assert a finder result with `expect(finder, findsOneWidget)` for one match or `findsNothing` for no match.
Create the widget tree before evaluating a finder-based assertion.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied widget test needs to prove that a particular label or keyed control exists after the tree is built. A finder describes what to locate, and an expectation states how many matches are acceptable. These are separate parts of a precise UI assertion.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Use `find.text('text')` to locate Text widgets displaying a given string. Use `find.byKey(key)` for a keyed widget or `find.byType(Type)` to locate widgets of a type. Assert a finder result with `expect(finder, findsOneWidget)` for one match or `findsNothing` for no match. Create the widget tree before evaluating a finder-based assertion.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The test assertion has three components: a built tree, a finder targeting the requirement, and a match-count expectation. In the Saved-label case, text defines the target and findsOneWidget defines the acceptable count. A key or type target uses its corresponding finder instead. FindsNothing is a deliberate absence expectation, not simply an assertion that something else exists. Trace these pieces in order so a test failure can be interpreted against the stated visible requirement. Do not treat the presence of any widget of a broad type as automatically proving a more specific label or keyed-control requirement.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content:
After creating the supplied widget tree, assert the illustrative Saved label with:
```dart
expect(find.text('Saved'), findsOneWidget);
```
`find.text('Saved')` targets Text widgets displaying Saved; findsOneWidget requires exactly one match. The assertion passes with one matching widget and fails with zero or more than one. To assert absence instead, use findsNothing. If the requirement identifies a keyed control, use find.byKey(key); if it identifies a widget type, use find.byType(Type). Choose the finder and expected count from the acceptance target, not whichever query happens to return something.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A finder is not itself an assertion that the required widget exists. The match expectation makes that claim testable. Also, evaluate finder-based assertions after constructing the tree; an unbuilt tree is not evidence about the supplied screen's intended content.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Write the expected visible result first, choose text, key, or type to identify it, and state the required match count. Compare a positive target and an absent target when the exercise supplies both. Keep the assertions on observable widgets rather than adding unrelated internal implementation checks.

teaching_blocks.content: A supplied form test should check what happens after input and a tap, not only whether the initial screen rendered. Test interactions and frame processing are separate steps: the action is simulated first, then the changed UI is allowed to render before assertion.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Simulate a tap using `await tester.tap(finder)` and text entry using `await tester.enterText(finder, text)`. Use `await tester.pump()` after an interaction to process a frame before checking the changed UI. Use `pumpAndSettle()` when a finite sequence of scheduled frames must finish, rather than assume a tap immediately rebuilds the test tree. Assert the observable UI after pumping to verify the interaction's effect.

teaching_blocks.content: Keep event simulation and output inspection on opposite sides of the pump. EnterText supplies the field input and tap supplies the action. context.concept_name: Handling expected Dart exceptions

coverage.learning_objective: Handle one expected exception without swallowing unrelated failures.

required_facts.statement: `throw` raises an exception and execution unwinds until a matching handler is found.
Handle a known exception type with `try { ... } on ExpectedType catch (e) { ... }` rather than catch all failures indiscriminately.
Use `catch (e, stackTrace)` when the handler needs both the exception and its trace.
Use `rethrow` when a caught failure must propagate to another handler instead of be swallowed.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied operation can fail with a known exception, and the feature needs a distinct failure outcome. Exception handling connects that raised failure to an appropriate handler instead of letting successful-path statements stand in for a result that was never produced.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: `throw` raises an exception and execution unwinds until a matching handler is found. Handle a known exception type with `try { ... } on ExpectedType catch (e) { ... }` rather than catch all failures indiscriminately. Use `catch (e, stackTrace)` when the handler needs both the exception and its trace. Use `rethrow` when a caught failure must propagate to another handler instead of be swallowed.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The success trace and failure trace leave the try block differently. A normal result permits its dependent successful path; a throw unwinds toward a matching handler. At that handler, decide from the supplied boundary contract whether to produce a failure outcome or rethrow to another handler. The known exception type makes that decision specific. If the trace is needed, the second catch parameter provides it. Keep caught-failure handling distinct from success: suppressing a failure without the required translation or propagation does not establish the successful result that the operation would have returned.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Place the supplied operation in a try block and use `on ExpectedType catch (e)` for its documented failure type. When that exception is thrown, execution unwinds until a matching handler is found; trace the handler rather than continuing as though the operation returned normally. If the supplied reporting contract needs the trace as well as the exception, use `catch (e, stackTrace)`. If another boundary must handle the caught failure, use rethrow so the failure propagates instead of being swallowed.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Catching a failure is not the same as resolving it successfully. A handler that suppresses a failure changes its propagation. Prefer the known exception type over indiscriminate handling that treats every failure as the same expected outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: For the supplied success and failure cases, identify which statements execute and which handler matches. Check whether the boundary should translate the failure or propagate it further. Keep this lesson about Dart exception control flow rather than inventing a retry policy or a new error-reporting service.

video_need.reason: A throw-to-handler trace makes unwinding and rethrow understandable.

The reporting handler receives both the exception and its trace and rethrows when required. An unrelated failure is not converted into the expected failure outcome.

coverage.learning_objective: Diagnose one runtime error using its first actionable application frame and framework context.

required_facts.statement: Flutter catches errors from framework callbacks and reports them through FlutterError.onError; the default handler presents them in device logs.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied Flutter callback fails and the report contains both framework and application frames. The reporting frame tells you how the error was surfaced; it is not necessarily the application statement that caused the failure. Read the report before selecting a source location to inspect.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Flutter catches errors from framework callbacks and reports them through FlutterError.onError; the default handler presents them in device logs. Read the reported exception and framework context, then inspect the call stack to locate the application call that caused the failure. Select the first relevant application frame and inspect that frame's source and variables rather than treat a framework reporting frame as the faulty application statement.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Use the report's parts as a sequence of evidence. The exception says what was reported, the framework context describes where it was surfaced, and the stack helps locate the relevant application call. The first relevant application frame gives the source and variables to inspect. This is different from assuming the top framework reporting frame is the defective statement. In the supplied callback failure, connect the observed exception with the chosen application source so the report explains a concrete call rather than prompting a broad rewrite. Keep FlutterError.onError's reporting role distinct from the source of the application failure.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature

Flutter catches framework-callback errors and reports them through FlutterError.onError; the default handler presents them in device logs. In the supplied stack, select the first relevant application frame and inspect that frame's source and variables. Connect the failing application call with the exception described in the report rather than editing the framework handler that presented it.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: The framework's reporting location is not automatically the faulty application statement. Nor does every frame in a long stack deserve an unrelated code change. The first relevant application frame is the focused starting point specified here.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Record the exception, its context, the selected application frame, and the source values that explain the failure. Keep the investigation tied to the supplied report. This applies error-report reading to Flutter without duplicating general debugging mechanics or changing the global Flutter error handler as a supposed repair.

context.concept_name: Future completion and asynchronous results

coverage.learning_objective: Consume one Future so pending, successful and failed completion are distinguished correctly.

required_facts.statement: A Future represents an operation that is uncompleted or completed with either a value or an error.
A `Future<T>` produces a value of type T on successful completion; the Future itself is not that eventual value.
Register a success callback with `future.then(onValue, onError: onError)` to distinguish successful and failed completion.

Future completion and callback execution are distinct: when `then` is registered on an already-completed Future, its callback is scheduled in a later microtask rather than called immediately, so a callback not yet having run does not mean the Future is still uncompleted.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied operation returns a Future rather than an order value immediately. The Future represents a completion outcome that may not yet exist. Distinguish the object representing the operation, the operation's completion, and the callback that later receives that outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: A Future represents an operation that is uncompleted or completed with either a value or an error. A `Future<T>` produces a value of type T on successful completion; the Future itself is not that eventual value. Register a success callback with `future.then(onValue, onError: onError)` to distinguish successful and failed completion. Future completion and callback execution are distinct: when `then` is registered on an already-completed Future, its callback is scheduled in a later microtask rather than called immediately, so a callback not yet having run does not mean the Future is still uncompleted.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Draw three points even for the already-completed Future case: completion, then registration, and callback execution. The last point occurs in a later microtask when then is registered after completion. That ordering explains the otherwise confusing observation that the Future is already completed but the callback has not yet run. For a newly uncompleted Future, distinguish the waiting representation from the eventual value-or-error outcome as well. Future<T> identifies the successful result type without turning the Future object into a value of T. The supplied onValue and onError callbacks receive distinct outcomes; lack of callback execution alone does not identify the completion state.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: For a supplied `Future<Order>`, successful completion yields an Order; the Future object is not itself that Order. Register the supplied success and failure callbacks using `future.then(onValue, onError: onError)`. Trace two outcomes: completion with an order goes to the success callback, while completion with an error goes to the failure callback. Also trace registration after the Future has already completed: the then callback is scheduled in a later microtask, not called immediately within registration.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A callback that has not run yet does not prove the Future is still uncompleted. Completion and callback execution are distinct. Likewise, having a Future<T> is not the same as already having a usable value of type T.

context.concept_name: Using async and await in Dart

coverage.learning_objective: Complete one awaited submit handler so success and expected failure reach the appropriate outcome.

required_facts.statement: Declare an asynchronous function with `async` and a return type such as `Future<T>` or `Future<void>`.

Await suspends the asynchronous function while other asynchronous work can run; it does not synchronously block the application waiting for the result.
Wrap an awaited operation in a typed try/catch to route its expected failure to the failure outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied function needs an order result before it can perform the next dependent statement. Async and await express that dependency while allowing other asynchronous work to run. The function waits for its result; the application is not synchronously blocked by that wait.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Declare an asynchronous function with `async` and a return type such as `Future<T>` or `Future<void>`. Inside an async function, use `await future` to obtain its completed value before executing dependent statements. Await suspends the asynchronous function while other asynchronous work can run; it does not synchronously block the application waiting for the result. Wrap an awaited operation in a typed try/catch to route its expected failure to the failure outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Follow only statements that depend on the awaited value. Their order is constrained by that dependency: obtain the completed value before using it. While the function is suspended, other asynchronous work can run, so the trace is not an application-wide synchronous pause. In the failure fixture, the awaited operation routes its expected failure to the typed handler instead of producing a value for those dependent statements. Check the declared Future return type against what the function is intended to complete with. This separates the function's asynchronous contract from the immediate synchronous appearance of statements written after await.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Await does not turn the whole application into a synchronous wait. It suspends the asynchronous function while other asynchronous work can run. Also, successful completion and expected failure are different paths; adding await is not itself a failure handler.

context.concept_name: Avoiding asynchronous updates after widget disposal

coverage.learning_objective: Guard one asynchronous completion so it never updates a disposed UI owner.

required_facts.statement: Calling setState after State disposal is an error.
Check `if (!mounted) return;` after awaited work and before a State update so a completion cannot update an unmounted owner.
Where possible, cancel work or detach the completion source when the owner is disposed rather than rely only on checking mounted.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied screen starts asynchronous work, then the user leaves before it finishes. Completion still needs to respect the lifetime of the State that would update the UI. A result being available does not prove its original owner is still mounted.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Calling setState after State disposal is an error. Check `if (!mounted) return;` after awaited work and before a State update so a completion cannot update an unmounted owner. Where possible, cancel work or detach the completion source when the owner is disposed rather than rely only on checking mounted.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Compare two timelines with the same asynchronous operation. In the first, the State remains mounted through completion, so the post-await guard permits the intended update. In the second, disposal occurs before completion, so the guard returns before setState. Without an onTimeout handler, exceeding the time limit completes the timeout future with TimeoutException. context.concept_name: Preventing stale request results from replacing current data

coverage.learning_objective: Prevent an older completion from overwriting the result of a newer request.

required_facts.statement: Asynchronous requests can finish in a different order from the order in which they were started.
Assign a distinct identity to a new request, store it as the current identity, and capture it in that request's completion callbacks.
Before publishing either a result or an error, compare the captured identity with the current identity and ignore a completion whose identity no longer matches.
FutureBuilder uses callback identities to ignore callbacks after replacement of its future or disposal of its State.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order search starts request A, then a changed selection starts request B. A can finish after B even though it started first. To present only the current request's outcome, compare completion identity with the identity currently owned by the feature.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Asynchronous requests can finish in a different order from the order in which they were started. Assign a distinct identity to a new request, store it as the current identity, and capture it in that request's completion callbacks. Before publishing either a result or an error, compare the captured identity with the current identity and ignore a completion whose identity no longer matches. FutureBuilder uses callback identities to ignore callbacks after replacement of its future or disposal of its State.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Use the same A/B labels for both successful and failed completions. If B is current, A's captured identity mismatches whether A returns data or an error. The comparison therefore precedes either publication. If B's captured identity matches the current identity, its outcome belongs to the current request under this mechanism. Request identity is separate from owner liveness: an owner may still be alive while A is obsolete. FutureBuilder's callback-identity behavior is an example of ignoring callbacks after replacement or disposal, not a statement that asynchronous work always completes in the order it began.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Assign a distinct identity when each supplied request begins, store it as current, and capture it in that request's completion callbacks. Suppose B becomes current and finishes first. When A later completes, its captured identity no longer matches, so ignore that completion. Make the comparison before publishing either a result or an error. FutureBuilder similarly uses callback identities to ignore callbacks after its Future is replaced or its State disposed.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Starting first does not guarantee finishing first. Also, filtering only successful data is incomplete: a stale error must not replace the current request's valid presentation either. Identity comparison applies before publishing either kind of outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Trace starts and completions in an intentionally reversed order. At each completion, write the captured identity beside the current identity and state whether publication is allowed. Check stale success and stale error cases. Keep this mechanism distinct from owner mounted checks: a still-live owner can still receive an obsolete request outcome.

context.concept_name: Dart inheritance and interface implementation for Flutter APIs

coverage.learning_objective: Implement one supplied Flutter API contract with all required members and valid polymorphic use.

required_facts.statement: Every class implicitly defines an interface consisting of its instance members and the interfaces it implements.
Declare `class Implementation implements Contract` and provide the APIs required by Contract rather than inherit its implementation.
A caller typed as Contract can use an implementing instance through the members exposed by that contract.
Use compatible member parameter and return types so the implementation satisfies the interface.

Declare `class Subclass extends Superclass` to inherit the superclass implementation; subclasses can override instance methods, getters, and setters, marking intentional overrides with `@override`, and an overriding method must accept the same number of positional parameters, use the same or broader parameter types and the same or narrower return type, and match whether the method is generic.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied application contract should accept more than one implementation without making callers depend on their internal code. In Dart, a class implicitly defines an interface through its instance members. Implements satisfies that interface; extends inherits an implementation.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Every class implicitly defines an interface consisting of its instance members and the interfaces it implements. Declare `class Implementation implements Contract` and provide the APIs required by Contract rather than inherit its implementation. A caller typed as Contract can use an implementing instance through the members exposed by that contract. Use compatible member parameter and return types so the implementation satisfies the interface. Declare `class Subclass extends Superclass` to inherit the superclass implementation; subclasses can override instance methods, getters, and setters, marking intentional overrides with `@override`, and an overriding method must accept the same number of positional parameters, use the same or broader parameter types and the same or narrower return type, and match whether the method is generic.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Check the contract from the caller's perspective. The caller can use the instance members exposed through Contract, so Implementation must provide compatible APIs even though it does not inherit their implementation through implements. For an overriding method in the extends case, compare positional-parameter count, parameter types, return type, and generic status with the original method. Same-or-broader accepted parameter types and same-or-narrower return types preserve the stated compatibility. Mark the intentional override with @override. An intentional method override is marked with @override and must preserve positional-parameter count, use the same or broader parameter types and the same or narrower return type, and match whether the method is generic.

context.concept_name: Controlling asynchronous completion in Flutter tests

coverage.learning_objective: Make one asynchronous test assert only after controlled work completes.

required_facts.statement: Await controlled asynchronous work before asserting a result that depends on its completion.
In a widget test, pump after the work completes to render the state change before checking the UI.
`pump(duration)` advances the test clock by the requested duration and schedules a frame; `pumpAndSettle()` pumps until no frames are scheduled.
Use a finite known completion point rather than pumpAndSettle when ongoing activity continually schedules frames.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied widget test depends on asynchronous work. An assertion before completion checks the wrong point in the scenario, and completion alone is not the same as rendering the resulting UI. Control the completion point, then pump the changed state before checking its visible result.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Await controlled asynchronous work before asserting a result that depends on its completion. In a widget test, pump after the work completes to render the state change before checking the UI. `pump(duration)` advances the test clock by the requested duration and schedules a frame; `pumpAndSettle()` pumps until no frames are scheduled. Use a finite known completion point rather than pumpAndSettle when ongoing activity continually schedules frames.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The test has an operation-completion point and a UI-rendering point. Awaiting controlled work establishes the former; pumping after completion establishes the frame needed before checking the changed UI. Pump with a duration also advances the test clock by that duration. PumpAndSettle instead uses the absence of scheduled frames as its stopping condition. If ongoing activity keeps scheduling frames, use the supplied finite known completion point rather than confusing that activity with work guaranteed to settle. Record exactly which completed work makes the assertion meaningful and which subsequent pump renders its effect.

In a widget test, pump after that completion so the new state renders. `pump(duration)` advances the test clock by the requested duration and schedules a frame; pumpAndSettle pumps until no frames are scheduled. If the supplied activity continually schedules frames, use its finite known completion point instead of expecting pumpAndSettle to finish that ongoing activity.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: More pumping is not a substitute for knowing what completion the assertion depends on. Also, pumpAndSettle is not a universal wait-for-anything operation: its stopping condition concerns scheduled frames, and ongoing activity may keep scheduling them.

context.concept_name: Returning a result from a screen

coverage.learning_objective: Return one selection result and correctly handle dismissal in its awaiting caller.

required_facts.statement: Await `Navigator.push<T>(...)` in the caller to obtain the route's completion result.
Return a selection using `Navigator.pop(context, selectedValue)` in the destination.
The returned value is nullable because route dismissal can occur without a selection; branch on null before using it as a selected value.
After awaiting route completion, check owner liveness before updating its UI.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied destination lets the user choose a value and return it to the caller. The route can also be dismissed without a selection. Treat the completion as a nullable result and check the caller's lifetime before applying a UI update.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Await `Navigator.push<T>(...)` in the caller to obtain the route's completion result. Return a selection using `Navigator.pop(context, selectedValue)` in the destination. The returned value is nullable because route dismissal can occur without a selection; branch on null before using it as a selected value. After awaiting route completion, check owner liveness before updating its UI.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The outward and return parts of the route have different data directions. The caller pushes and awaits completion; the destination pops with the selected value; the caller checks the nullable result and owner liveness before using it to update UI. If the route is dismissed without selection, the null branch represents that absence rather than a model with invented default fields. If the caller was disposed during the await, a non-null result still cannot justify an owner update. Trace those conditions independently so a successful selection is not used as proof that both nullability and lifetime checks have been satisfied.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: In the caller, await `Navigator.push<T>(...)`. In the destination, return the supplied selection with `Navigator.pop(context, selectedValue)`. After completion, branch on null before treating the result as a selected value. For a State owner, apply the taught post-await liveness check before changing its UI. Trace a confirmed selection and a dismissal separately: the first supplies the value; the second must follow the specified no-selection behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Route completion does not guarantee a selection was returned. Dismissal can produce null. Nor does a valid selected value prove the caller's UI owner still exists after the await.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Record the route's expected result type, the destination's returned value, and the caller's null branch. Then check owner liveness before the supplied update. Keep constructor inputs and returned route results distinct: one supplies data to a screen; the other delivers a completion value back to its caller.

video_need.reason: Selection versus dismissal and the returned result are useful changing navigation outcomes.

practice_anchor.success: A confirmed selection reaches the caller and updates its UI only while its State is mounted. Dismissal follows the no-selection branch without changing the existing selection. Completion after caller disposal does not trigger a UI update.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied app uses locations to describe destinations. GoRouter maps each configured path to screen configuration, and navigation to a location uses the stack configured for that location rather than always adding one route on top of the current stack.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Create a GoRouter with a list of `GoRoute(path: ..., builder: ...)` definitions mapping locations to screen configurations. teaching_blocks.content: For each location, follow the configured path to its builder and screen configuration. MaterialApp.router connects the application to that GoRouter. context.concept_name: Reading and validating route parameters

coverage.learning_objective: Validate and consume one route parameter while rejecting invalid values.

required_facts.statement: Declare a path parameter with a colon-prefixed segment such as `:parameterName`, then read it from `state.pathParameters['parameterName']`.
Read query-string values from `state.uri.queryParameters['parameterName']`.
Check that a nullable route parameter is present before converting it; for an integer contract use `int.tryParse(rawValue)` and reject a null parse result before constructing the destination.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied detail location carries an identity in its path and an optional value in its query string. Route parameters arrive as values to validate, not as an already-constructed typed model input. Presence and conversion are separate checks.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Declare a path parameter with a colon-prefixed segment such as `:parameterName`, then read it from `state.pathParameters['parameterName']`. Read query-string values from `state.uri.queryParameters['parameterName']`. Check that a nullable route parameter is present before converting it; for an integer contract use `int.tryParse(rawValue)` and reject a null parse result before constructing the destination.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The integer-route example has three useful gates: raw lookup, presence, and valid parse. An absent lookup stops before conversion. A present malformed string fails int.tryParse and must be rejected before the destination is constructed. A present valid string supplies the typed identity only after parsing succeeds. Keep the path map and query map distinct when doing the first lookup. This sequence prevents a nullable or malformed value from being treated as the destination's required integer simply because the URL reached the router. Use the same prescribed identity contract for all three supplied parameter cases.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Declare the supplied path segment with a colon prefix, such as `:orderId`, and read `state.pathParameters['orderId']`. Read query values through `state.uri.queryParameters['parameterName']`. For an integer identity contract, first check that the raw nullable value is present, then use `int.tryParse(rawValue)`. Reject a null parse result before constructing the destination. Compare illustrative raw values '12', an absent value, and 'twelve': only the valid parsed identity satisfies that integer contract.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A present string is not automatically a valid integer. Likewise, an absent parameter must be handled before conversion. Path parameters and query-string parameters come from different maps; do not assume one lookup retrieves both kinds.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Trace the location to the raw value, the presence check, and the parse result. Construct the destination only after the contract's required checks succeed. Keep fallback routing in its own lesson; this target is validation before the typed destination is created.

context.concept_name: Handling unknown or invalid routes

coverage.learning_objective: Implement one safe fallback for an unrecognized application location.

required_facts.statement: An unmatched or unusable location can produce a GoException rather than a valid destination.
Provide `errorBuilder: (context, state) => ErrorScreen(state.error)` to render a deliberate fallback for a routing exception.
`onException` can choose a recovery navigation and takes precedence over errorBuilder and errorPageBuilder when provided.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied location may fail to match or be unusable. The app needs a deliberate routing failure outcome rather than treating every incoming location as a valid destination. GoRouter exposes exception handling choices with an explicit precedence rule.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: An unmatched or unusable location can produce a GoException rather than a valid destination. Provide `errorBuilder: (context, state) => ErrorScreen(state.error)` to render a deliberate fallback for a routing exception. `onException` can choose a recovery navigation and takes precedence over errorBuilder and errorPageBuilder when provided.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Choose the configured recovery mechanism before predicting the failure screen. If errorBuilder is the applicable choice, it receives state.error and constructs the deliberate ErrorScreen. If onException is provided, it takes precedence over errorBuilder and errorPageBuilder and can choose recovery navigation. This is why the exercise should not promise that every configured builder will run on the same exception. Trace the unmatched or unusable location into its routing exception and then through the actual configured choice. Keep the recovery outcome distinct from the original requested screen so the app does not present a routing failure as successful destination resolution.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: For the supplied routing exception, use `errorBuilder: (context, state) => ErrorScreen(state.error)` to render the designated fallback. If the exercise instead supplies onException to choose recovery navigation, remember that it takes precedence over errorBuilder and errorPageBuilder. Trace an unmatched or unusable location to the GoException outcome and then to the configured recovery mechanism. Do not describe the fallback screen as though the requested destination had been successfully built.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Providing several recovery callbacks does not mean they all execute in parallel. The supplied onException takes precedence over the error builders. An unmatched or unusable location is a routing failure, not evidence of a valid but empty destination.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Check the failing location and identify which recovery API the supplied configuration actually uses. Verify the designated fallback or recovery navigation occurs. Keep the fallback behavior deliberate and bounded rather than inventing a default destination that the exercise contract does not specify.

The documented app-link or universal-link setup addresses the platform part; the configured GoRouter path addresses the in-app part. Verify both through the supplied URL fixtures. Cold-start and running-app entry are separate observations because initial platform navigation differs between Android and iOS. context.concept_name: Predictable Android and iOS back behavior

coverage.learning_objective: Implement one back-handling policy that preserves the supplied route and unsaved-edit requirements.

required_facts.statement: Use PopScope around a route and set `canPop` from the current back-navigation policy to allow or block route dismissal.
`onPopInvokedWithResult` reports an attempted pop, and its `didPop` value indicates whether the route actually popped.
When unsaved changes block dismissal, handle `onPopInvokedWithResult: (didPop, result) async { ... }`, return if didPop is true, and otherwise obtain confirmation before performing an allowed pop.

On iOS with CupertinoRouteTransitionMixin, `canPop: false` prevents gesture detection and its callback is not invoked for that gesture; Android reports a blocked system-back attempt with didPop false.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied edit route has unsaved changes and must apply a back-navigation policy. PopScope controls whether dismissal is allowed, while its callback reports whether an attempted pop actually happened. Keep the policy decision separate from the attempt's result.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Use PopScope around a route and set `canPop` from the current back-navigation policy to allow or block route dismissal. `onPopInvokedWithResult` reports an attempted pop, and its `didPop` value indicates whether the route actually popped. When unsaved changes block dismissal, handle `onPopInvokedWithResult: (didPop, result) async { ... }`, return if didPop is true, and otherwise obtain confirmation before performing an allowed pop. On iOS with CupertinoRouteTransitionMixin, `canPop: false` prevents gesture detection and its callback is not invoked for that gesture; Android reports a blocked system-back attempt with didPop false.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Use canPop as the policy input and didPop as the reported result, not as interchangeable booleans. In the callback, didPop true means the route already popped, so return. When the attempt is reported as not popped, follow the supplied confirmation policy before an allowed pop. Keep the iOS CupertinoRouteTransitionMixin qualification beside that trace: canPop false prevents gesture detection and no callback is invoked for that gesture. Android's blocked system-back attempt reports didPop false instead. The expected test evidence therefore differs by platform; absence of an iOS gesture callback is not an unreported Android-style successful dismissal.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Wrap the route with PopScope and set canPop from the supplied policy. In `onPopInvokedWithResult: (didPop, result) async { ... }`, return when didPop is true; otherwise obtain the required confirmation before performing an allowed pop. Trace Android's blocked system-back attempt as didPop false. Separately consider iOS with CupertinoRouteTransitionMixin: with canPop false, the gesture is not detected and that gesture does not invoke the callback. The two platform cases must not be presented as identical callback sequences.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: The callback reports an attempt; it does not prove the route popped. Also, a blocked Android system-back callback does not imply an iOS gesture will invoke the same callback under CupertinoRouteTransitionMixin.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Test the allowed and blocked policies, then inspect didPop for attempts that report it. Apply confirmation only to the blocked, not-already-popped case specified by the exercise. Keep the platform distinction visible and avoid interpreting an absent iOS gesture callback as an Android-style didPop false report.

An already-completed pop causes no additional confirmation or pop. teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Compare evidence in two groups. Capability and supported platforms answer whether the package can serve the feature on its targets. context.concept_name: Pinning compatible Flutter dependencies

coverage.learning_objective: Resolve one ordinary dependency conflict with compatible constraints and a reproducible lockfile.

required_facts.statement: Dependency constraints specify the allowed versions from which pub must resolve a mutually compatible dependency graph.
Caret syntax permits compatible versions up to the next breaking-version boundary, rather than pinning one exact version.
Adjust incompatible constraints to a mutually supported range, then run `flutter pub get` to resolve dependencies.
The application's pubspec.lock records the resolved versions; retain it to make application dependency resolution reproducible.
Forcing an unsupported version through dependency_overrides can break the application and is not proof of compatibility.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied dependency conflict means the requested versions cannot currently form the required compatible graph. Constraints describe allowed versions; the resolver must find versions that satisfy those relationships together. Forcing one version is not proof that it works with the rest.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Dependency constraints specify the allowed versions from which pub must resolve a mutually compatible dependency graph. Caret syntax permits compatible versions up to the next breaking-version boundary, rather than pinning one exact version. Adjust incompatible constraints to a mutually supported range, then run `flutter pub get` to resolve dependencies. The application's pubspec.lock records the resolved versions; retain it to make application dependency resolution reproducible. Forcing an unsupported version through dependency_overrides can break the application and is not proof of compatibility.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Read constraints as allowed ranges and the lockfile as recorded resolution. Pub must resolve a mutually compatible dependency graph within the constraints. A caret range is broader than a single pinned version but still bounded by its breaking-version boundary. If the supplied conflict has no mutually supported range as written, adjust it using the supported compatibility information and resolve again. An override that forces an unsupported version does not supply the missing compatibility evidence. Keep the application's resolved lockfile so the chosen versions are recorded, while avoiding a promise that every future range adjustment or forced version is safe.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Read the supplied conflicting constraints and adjust them to a mutually supported range. Run `flutter pub get` to resolve the dependencies. Caret syntax allows compatible versions up to the next breaking-version boundary rather than pinning one exact version. For the application, retain pubspec.lock because it records the resolved versions used for reproducible resolution. Compare the intended allowed range with the actual resolved versions rather than treating the constraint text as a list of already-installed versions.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A caret constraint is not an exact pin. Also, dependency_overrides can force an unsupported version and break the app; that forced resolution is not evidence of compatibility. The application's lockfile and dependency constraints describe different parts of the resolution story.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Record the original conflict, supported constraint adjustment, pub get outcome, and resolved lockfile values. Verify the adjustment is based on a mutually supported range in the supplied compatibility information. Keep the lesson on resolution and reproducibility rather than introducing unsupported upgrade promises or general source-control procedures.
