context.concept_name: Requesting runtime permission at the point of need

coverage.learning_objective: Request one capability permission at its supplied feature's point of need.

required_facts.statement: Read a capability's current status with `await Permission.capability.status`.
Call `await Permission.capability.request()` when the feature needs authorization and use the returned status to decide whether to proceed.
A request returns the new permission status; if permission was already granted, requesting it again does not display another authorization dialog.
Limit permission requests to access relevant to the requested feature and respect the user's decision.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied feature needs permission before accessing a mobile capability. Read the current status and request authorization when the feature needs it; then decide from the returned status whether the action can proceed.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Read a capability's current status with `await Permission.capability.status`. Call `await Permission.capability.request()` when the feature needs authorization and use the returned status to decide whether to proceed. A request returns the new permission status; if permission was already granted, requesting it again does not display another authorization dialog. Limit permission requests to access relevant to the requested feature and respect the user's decision.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The permission trace has an intent, a status, a request when needed, and a result-dependent action. The supplied feature determines why authorization is relevant; the returned status determines whether that feature can proceed. Requesting an already-granted permission produces its status without displaying another authorization dialog. This prevents the example from teaching a dialog as the mandatory observable result of every request call. Keep the user's decision in the branch outcome, and keep the request limited to feature-relevant access. Use the contract's non-proceeding behavior when authorization is not granted rather than treating the request call itself as permission.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Use `await Permission.capability.status` with the supplied capability in place of the placeholder. When authorization is needed for the feature, call `await Permission.capability.request()` and inspect its returned status. If permission was already granted, requesting again does not display another authorization dialog. Trace a granted outcome into the allowed feature action and another outcome into the specified non-proceeding behavior. Limit requests to access relevant to the requested feature and respect the user's choice.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Calling request is not itself proof that authorization was granted. The returned status determines whether to proceed. Also, repeated requests for an already-granted permission do not promise a new dialog each time.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Record the capability, current status, reason the feature needs authorization, request result, and resulting branch. Keep this example on the request decision; the distinct meanings of denied, restricted, and permanently denied are developed next.

context.concept_name: Handling permission denial and restricted access

coverage.learning_objective: Implement one denial fallback that distinguishes recoverable denial from restricted access without repeated prompting.

required_facts.statement: A denied status can mean permission was not requested or was denied before; restricted means the operating system limits access, such as through parental controls.
A permanentlyDenied request result means the user must change permission in system settings rather than receive another prompt.
Branch on the request result and provide an unavailable-feature fallback for denied or restricted access rather than continue as if access were granted.
Offer `openAppSettings()` for an appropriate permanently denied case instead of repeatedly presenting a permission prompt.
On Android, the status getter reports denied even for permanent denial, so use the request result when distinguishing permanent denial.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied permission request does not grant access, and the feature needs a respectful fallback. Denied, restricted, and permanentlyDenied have different meanings, so read the right status source before deciding whether another prompt or settings action is appropriate.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: A denied status can mean permission was not requested or was denied before; restricted means the operating system limits access, such as through parental controls. A permanentlyDenied request result means the user must change permission in system settings rather than receive another prompt. Branch on the request result and provide an unavailable-feature fallback for denied or restricted access rather than continue as if access were granted. Offer `openAppSettings()` for an appropriate permanently denied case instead of repeatedly presenting a permission prompt. On Android, the status getter reports denied even for permanent denial, so use the request result when distinguishing permanent denial.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the source of each status beside its meaning. A request result can identify permanentlyDenied, which calls for a settings change rather than another prompt. Android's status getter still reports denied for permanent denial, so a getter-only trace cannot establish that distinction. Restricted is an operating-system limitation, not the same description as a user denial. For denied or restricted access, the supplied unavailable-feature fallback is the outcome rather than the protected action. When settings is appropriate for permanent denial, offer it deliberately instead of running a repeating permission prompt sequence as though the status guaranteed another dialog.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Branch on the request result. A denied result can reflect not-yet-requested or previously denied access; restricted means the OS limits access, such as through parental controls. Provide the specified unavailable-feature fallback rather than continuing as granted. For an appropriate permanentlyDenied result, offer `openAppSettings()` because the user must change permission in settings. On Android, the status getter reports denied even for permanent denial, so use the request result to distinguish that permanent-denial case.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Android's denied status getter is not enough to prove a fresh prompt is possible. Also, repeatedly requesting a permanently denied permission does not replace the needed system-settings change. Denied and OS-restricted access should not be treated as authorization.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Trace each supplied non-granted request result to its intended fallback or settings option. Keep the source of the status explicit, especially on Android. Check that no protected feature action continues in the denied or restricted branches, while preserving the user's decision rather than inventing an automatic permission recovery.

video_need.reason: Different request results and a settings recovery path benefit from platform-state demonstrations.

context.concept_name: Handling unsupported or unavailable device capabilities

coverage.learning_objective: Add one fallback that works when a supplied device capability is unsupported or unavailable.

required_facts.statement: Device and platform capabilities are conditional; the application should not assume the same features are available on all targets.
Use a capability check or the adapter's availability result and select an alternative behavior when the capability is absent rather than invoke it unconditionally.
For a permission-backed service, authorization and service availability are separate checks; permission_handler exposes `serviceStatus.isEnabled` for supported services.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied target may lack a capability or have its backing service disabled even when permission exists. Authorization and service availability answer different questions, so the feature must not infer both from one granted status.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Device and platform capabilities are conditional; the application should not assume the same features are available on all targets. Use a capability check or the adapter's availability result and select an alternative behavior when the capability is absent rather than invoke it unconditionally. For a permission-backed service, authorization and service availability are separate checks; permission_handler exposes `serviceStatus.isEnabled` for supported services.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The feature has at least two distinct questions in the permission-backed service example: is access authorized, and is the service enabled? Device/platform capability adds the supplied availability question where applicable. A granted status answers authorization, not all of those questions together. ServiceStatus.isEnabled is exposed for supported services; do not turn that into a universal check for every capability. Use the adapter's supplied availability result where that is the feature's contract. In the absent-capability or disabled-service fixture, choose the alternative behavior before invoking the unavailable feature rather than presenting a failed invocation as the normal availability test.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Use the supplied capability check or adapter availability result before invoking the feature. If the capability is absent, choose the specified alternative behavior. For a supported permission-backed service, permission_handler exposes `serviceStatus.isEnabled`; check that separately from authorization. Trace a target with authorized but unavailable service and a target where the feature is available. The result should follow the feature's supplied availability contract, not an assumption that all mobile devices offer the same capability.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Granted authorization does not establish enabled service availability. Nor does successful operation on one target prove that every required target has the capability. Keep those checks separate.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Record target capability, authorization, service availability where supported, and chosen behavior. Test the supplied unavailable case as well as the available case. Use only the adapter or service checks documented for the supplied feature instead of inventing a universal availability API.

context.concept_name: Choosing preferences, files or an embedded database for app data

coverage.learning_objective: Select and justify one storage mechanism for the supplied durability and access requirements.

required_facts.statement: Key-value preferences fit small, simple non-critical settings and support int, double, bool, String, and List<String>.
An application file fits data that the application reads and writes as file contents.
SQLite is a local database suitable for large amounts of structured local data, rather than a few simple settings or a file of application-managed contents.
Choose the mechanism according to the data shape and retrieval operations; preferences are not suitable for critical data because durable persistence is not guaranteed when a write returns.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied feature keeps a simple display setting, a text document, and a collection of structured local records. Storage choice follows data shape and retrieval operations. These needs do not all belong in the same local mechanism merely because they are stored on the device.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Key-value preferences fit small, simple non-critical settings and support int, double, bool, String, and List<String>. An application file fits data that the application reads and writes as file contents. SQLite is a local database suitable for large amounts of structured local data, rather than a few simple settings or a file of application-managed contents. Choose the mechanism according to the data shape and retrieval operations; preferences are not suitable for critical data because durable persistence is not guaranteed when a write returns.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Explain each selection by the operations the feature needs. The display setting has a small simple typed value and is non-critical, matching preferences. The text document is read and written as file contents, matching an application file. The structured local collection fits SQLite's database role. These are contextual examples of the supplied mechanisms rather than an exhaustive taxonomy of all possible storage systems. Keep the preferences durability limitation beside the importance decision: an awaited setter does not guarantee durable persistence when it returns. If the proposed value is critical, do not let its small size alone justify preferences.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Use key-value preferences for the supplied small, simple non-critical setting. Use an application file when the contract is reading and writing file contents. Use SQLite for the supplied large structured local collection and its retrieval needs. Preferences support int, double, bool, String, and List<String>, but their write completion does not guarantee durable persistence. That limitation matters if a proposed setting is actually critical data rather than a convenience value.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Awaiting a preferences write does not make preferences suitable for critical data. Also, SQLite is not required merely because a value must be kept locally; the choice depends on its shape and required retrieval operations.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Describe each supplied value's shape, importance, and read/write needs, then choose the corresponding mechanism. Keep the identity predicate in the delete operation so only the intended record is removed. Use the returned affected-row count to determine whether a row matched the deletion. A subsequent query for the deleted identity should return no row while queries for other identities still return their records.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The deletion proof has a removed side and a retained side. The selected identity should no longer be returned by a query, while other identities should still return their records. The affected-row count connects the operation with whether a row matched, but the follow-up reads establish the stated presence/absence outcomes. Keeping the identity predicate gives the action its scope; omitting it changes which records the operation can remove. Use the same fixture identities before and after deletion so the preservation check is meaningful, and do not equate a zero-match call with proof of removing a known existing record.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Call `await db.delete(tableName, where: 'id = ?', whereArgs: [id])` with the selected identity. Keep the predicate and inspect the affected-row count to see whether a row matched. Query the deleted identity afterward: it should return no row. Query the other supplied identities too when checking preservation; they should still return their records. The exercise verifies both removal and the boundary around that removal.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Deleting the intended record is not the same as clearing the table. Dropping the identity predicate changes the operation's scope. Also, a zero-match deletion should not be presented as proof that a previously existing row was removed.

Keep the verification tied to the supplied rows and avoid adding a new cleanup policy that would remove more records than the contract allows.

Update onCreate to create the latest schema for fresh installations as well as add the upgrade path for existing installations. context.concept_name: Handling ordinary persistence failures

coverage.learning_objective: Handle one failed write without falsely reporting committed durable state.

required_facts.statement: Await each persistence operation and report success only after it completes successfully.
An exception thrown out of a transaction causes rollback; completing its callback without an exception commits the transaction.
Do not suppress a persistence exception inside the transaction when rollback is required; propagate it to the boundary that translates failure for the caller.
Use the transaction object for operations inside `db.transaction((txn) async { ... })`, rather than call the database object and deadlock.
Catch expected SQL failures with `on DatabaseException catch (e)` at the persistence boundary and return or propagate the application-facing failure rather than report success.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied multi-operation persistence action must not report success if a required operation fails. A transaction commits or rolls back according to whether its callback completes without an exception. Failure propagation is therefore part of the persistence result, not just reporting style.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Await each persistence operation and report success only after it completes successfully. An exception thrown out of a transaction causes rollback; completing its callback without an exception commits the transaction. Do not suppress a persistence exception inside the transaction when rollback is required; propagate it to the boundary that translates failure for the caller. Use the transaction object for operations inside `db.transaction((txn) async { ... })`, rather than call the database object and deadlock. Catch expected SQL failures with `on DatabaseException catch (e)` at the persistence boundary and return or propagate the application-facing failure rather than report success.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Use exception propagation to predict the transaction result. If the callback completes without an exception, it commits; if an exception escapes, it rolls back. Catching a required failure inside the callback and suppressing it changes that prediction, so propagation is part of the operation's correctness. Within the transaction, use txn for operations rather than the database object, which can deadlock in this pattern. At the application-facing boundary, expected DatabaseException handling turns a persistence failure into the prescribed failure result. Trace each operation's awaited completion so a success message cannot precede an unfinished or failed required write.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Await each operation and use the transaction object for calls inside `db.transaction((txn) async { ... })`. A thrown exception leaving the callback causes rollback; completing it without an exception commits. Do not suppress a required rollback failure inside the callback. At the persistence boundary, catch expected SQL failures with `on DatabaseException catch (e)` and translate or propagate the application-facing failure instead of claiming success. Calling the database object inside the transaction rather than txn can deadlock.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Catching and swallowing a persistence exception inside the transaction is not a rollback request. The callback can then complete without an exception. Also, database-object calls and transaction-object calls are not interchangeable within the stated transaction pattern.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Trace a fully successful fixture and one with a required operation failure. Mark which object performs each transaction call, whether the exception leaves the callback, and what outcome the caller receives. Verify success is reported only after successful completion; keep generic transaction theory outside this Dart/sqflite application lesson.

Success is returned only after the transaction completes successfully.

context.concept_name: Consuming Stream events with a managed subscription lifetime

coverage.learning_objective: Consume one event stream and cancel its subscription when its owner is disposed.

required_facts.statement: Use `stream.listen(onData, onError: onError, onDone: onDone)` to receive repeated data, error, and completion events.
The listen call returns a StreamSubscription that represents the listener's ownership of the subscription.
Store the subscription and cancel it when its owner no longer needs updates; a canceled listener stops receiving events.
If a State-owned source changes, cancel the old subscription before listening to the replacement and cancel the remaining subscription in dispose.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied source emits repeated updates rather than one completion. Listening creates a StreamSubscription with an owner, and that owner must stop receiving updates when its need ends or its State-owned source is replaced.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Use `stream.listen(onData, onError: onError, onDone: onDone)` to receive repeated data, error, and completion events. The listen call returns a StreamSubscription that represents the listener's ownership of the subscription. Store the subscription and cancel it when its owner no longer needs updates; a canceled listener stops receiving events. If a State-owned source changes, cancel the old subscription before listening to the replacement and cancel the remaining subscription in dispose.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: A repeated-event source has a listening relationship that outlasts one data callback. The returned StreamSubscription is the handle representing that listener's ownership. Data, error, and done callbacks describe event handling; cancellation describes ending the relationship. In the State-source replacement, stop the old listener before starting the new one and cancel the final listener at disposal. These are lifetime transitions, not additional data events. Keep the old and replacement sources labeled throughout the trace so canceling one is not mistaken for ending the other. The supplied owner determines when the subscription is no longer needed.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Listen using `stream.listen(onData, onError: onError, onDone: onDone)` for the supplied data, error, and completion handlers. Store the returned StreamSubscription. When the owner no longer needs updates, cancel it; a canceled listener stops receiving events. If a State-owned source changes, cancel the old subscription before listening to the replacement, then cancel the remaining subscription in dispose. Trace the old and new subscriptions separately so only the intended source remains listened to.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A stream listener is not merely a callback with no lifetime responsibility. Listen returns the subscription that represents this listener's ownership. Replacing a State-owned source without canceling the old subscription does not satisfy the stated replacement sequence.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Identify the subscription owner, where listen starts, what change replaces the source, and where cancellation happens. Check data, error, and completion events against the supplied contract. Keep the example on stream lifetime management before applying it to authentication or messaging services.

context.concept_name: Recognizing that client code is not a service security boundary

coverage.learning_objective: Correct one supplied access decision so it relies on service enforcement rather than a bypassable client check.

required_facts.statement: Server-enforced access rules are the authority for whether a remote data operation is permitted.
A client-side validation rule or hidden UI action does not substitute for a rule that denies the operation at the remote data boundary.
An allow-all test configuration permits anyone to read and overwrite data, so remove it and enforce the intended access policy before production use.
Keep client checks for user feedback, but require the backend policy to protect the same operation even if those checks are bypassed.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied app hides a protected action in its UI, but remote access still needs server-enforced rules. Client checks guide the user; they are not the authority that determines whether a remote operation is permitted.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Server-enforced access rules are the authority for whether a remote data operation is permitted. A client-side validation rule or hidden UI action does not substitute for a rule that denies the operation at the remote data boundary. An allow-all test configuration permits anyone to read and overwrite data, so remove it and enforce the intended access policy before production use. Keep client checks for user feedback, but require the backend policy to protect the same operation even if those checks are bypassed.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The client and server checks have different authorities. Client validation can explain to a user why an action is unavailable, but the remote policy must still protect the operation if that client check is bypassed. The supplied deny fixture tests that boundary. An allow-all test configuration permits anyone to read and overwrite data, so it cannot be relabeled as a protected production setup. Keep the intended access policy in force while evaluating permitted and denied operations. This is the security distinction the learner must carry into later service use; it does not require inventing backend code or new rule conditions here.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the supplied client validation and UI checks for user feedback, while requiring the backend policy to deny the protected operation when its access conditions are not met. An allow-all test configuration permits anyone to read and overwrite data, so remove it and enforce the intended policy before production. Trace a disallowed operation at the remote boundary even if the client-side action is bypassed. The policy and fixtures are supplied; the lesson does not require implementing a server.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A hidden action is not a security boundary. Neither client validation nor a route that is difficult to reach substitutes for server-enforced access denial. An allow-all testing configuration must not be treated as production protection.

Check the supplied permitted and denied operation fixtures, including the denial expected when client checks are bypassed. Keep the explanation on the authority boundary rather than teaching new server APIs or promising protection from unspecified rules.

teaching_blocks.content: A supplied Flutter app uses Firebase services and must initialize them with the configuration for the current target. Initialization order connects the Flutter binding, supplied options, asynchronous Firebase startup, and the later service-using application code.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Use the target-appropriate Firebase options supplied by the generated firebase_options.dart configuration. Await `Firebase.initializeApp(options: DefaultFirebaseOptions.currentPlatform)` before starting application code that uses Firebase services. teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Startup ordering has a clear dependency: code using Firebase services comes after completed Firebase initialization. The binding initialization precedes that asynchronous startup, and the generated current-platform options provide the target configuration. Rebuild/run includes the configured platform integration. required_facts.statement: Address the intended document with `db.collection(collectionPath).doc(documentId)`; keep that reference for both the read and the write.

teaching_blocks.content: A supplied edit screen reads and writes one Firestore document. Its reference and field mapping define the scope of the edit. Ordinary set can overwrite the addressed document, so a partial edit that must preserve other fields needs the stated merge behavior.

teaching_blocks.content: Address the intended document with `db.collection(collectionPath).doc(documentId)`; keep that reference for both the read and the write. teaching_blocks.content: The reference identifies the same document throughout the edit. A read obtains its snapshot and requires absence checks before model mapping. context.concept_name: Handling service access failures under supplied security rules

coverage.learning_objective: Handle one denied service operation under supplied rules without broadening authorization.

required_facts.statement: Cloud Firestore Security Rules evaluate mobile and web client requests and deny an operation when its access conditions are not satisfied.
Catch an expected Firebase failure around the awaited operation with `on FirebaseException catch (e)` and inspect its code to distinguish the documented denied-access outcome.
Translate a denied operation into an application-facing access failure rather than treat it as successful data retrieval or mutation.
Do not recover by making the rules allow all access: handle the denied operation under the existing policy and obtain authorized access only through the policy's permitted conditions.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied Firestore operation is denied by its Security Rules. This is an access failure under the current policy, not a successful empty read or completed edit. Translate the documented failure without weakening the policy to make the request pass.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Cloud Firestore Security Rules evaluate mobile and web client requests and deny an operation when its access conditions are not satisfied. Catch an expected Firebase failure around the awaited operation with `on FirebaseException catch (e)` and inspect its code to distinguish the documented denied-access outcome. Translate a denied operation into an application-facing access failure rather than treat it as successful data retrieval or mutation. Do not recover by making the rules allow all access: handle the denied operation under the existing policy and obtain authorized access only through the policy's permitted conditions.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The access-denial trace should retain the policy's meaning at every step. Rules evaluate the request, a denied operation produces the documented Firebase failure, the typed handler checks its code, and the client reports an access failure. None of those steps produces successful data or a successful mutation. Nor does client recovery include making rules allow all. Under the supplied policy, authorized access must meet permitted conditions. Keep the exception-code distinction tied to the documented outcome instead of broadly labeling every FirebaseException as a denial, and keep the denied-operation UI separate from an empty successful result.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Wrap the awaited operation in `on FirebaseException catch (e)` and inspect its code for the documented denied-access outcome. Firestore Security Rules evaluate mobile and web client requests and deny operations whose access conditions are unsatisfied. Map that denial to the supplied application-facing access failure. Obtain authorized access only through the existing policy's permitted conditions; do not switch rules to allow all as a recovery.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A caught denial is not successful retrieval or mutation. Making the rules allow all changes the security policy rather than handling the denied operation. Keep the policy authority separate from the client-facing error message.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Trace the denied fixture from request to exception code to the application's failure presentation. Compare it with an authorized outcome only under the supplied policy conditions. Keep error handling typed and bounded to the documented failure rather than treating every Firebase failure as this same denial.

context.concept_name: Defining local-data retention and deletion behavior

coverage.learning_objective: Implement one supplied retention policy so account changes delete only the appropriate local data.

required_facts.statement: Observe account transitions from the session stream and apply the retention policy to the previous owner's local data rather than assume a new account owns it.
Identify the local keys or records assigned to the departing account and separately identify device-wide or other-owner data that the retention policy preserves.
Remove selected preference or secure-storage keys with `remove(key)` or `delete(key: key)`, rather than clear an entire store containing data that must be retained.
For database-backed account data, pass the ownership predicate and bound arguments to `db.delete(tableName, where: ownershipPredicate, whereArgs: ownerValues)` so unrelated records remain.
Await the policy-directed deletions and verify that the departing account's selected data is absent while retained data remains.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied app changes accounts, and the retention policy removes some departing-account data while preserving device-wide and other-owner data. Account transition does not transfer ownership of old local values to the new account.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Observe account transitions from the session stream and apply the retention policy to the previous owner's local data rather than assume a new account owns it. Identify the local keys or records assigned to the departing account and separately identify device-wide or other-owner data that the retention policy preserves. Remove selected preference or secure-storage keys with `remove(key)` or `delete(key: key)`, rather than clear an entire store containing data that must be retained. For database-backed account data, pass the ownership predicate and bound arguments to `db.delete(tableName, where: ownershipPredicate, whereArgs: ownerValues)` so unrelated records remain. Await the policy-directed deletions and verify that the departing account's selected data is absent while retained data remains.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The departing account, other accounts, and device-wide data have separate ownership categories under the retention policy. Identify those categories before deletion so the removable set is deliberate. Selected preference or secure keys are removed individually; database rows use the ownership predicate and bound arguments. Await those operations, then inspect both the selected old-owner data and the retained data. Checking only that some data disappeared would miss an accidental wipe of preserved records. The transition stream supplies the account change, but the retention policy supplies what should be removed; neither implies automatic transfer of old data to the next account.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Observe transitions from the session stream and identify the previous owner's keys or records under the supplied policy. Identify retained data separately. Remove selected preference keys with remove and secure-storage keys with delete, rather than clearing a mixed store. For account rows, call `db.delete(tableName, where: ownershipPredicate, whereArgs: ownerValues)` with the policy's ownership predicate and bound values. Await the directed deletions, then verify the selected old-owner data is absent and retained data remains.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Clearing an entire store is not equivalent to policy-directed account cleanup when that store includes data that must remain. Also, a new signed-in account does not automatically become the owner of the previous account's local records.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Before cleanup, list the departing owner's removable data and the policy-preserved data. After awaited deletion, compare both lists with actual remaining keys or records. Keep the ownership predicate tied to the supplied account identity and retention contract; do not invent a blanket sign-out wipe policy.

context.concept_name: Recording appropriate analytics events with user privacy controls

coverage.learning_objective: Record one non-sensitive event only under the supplied consent and privacy controls.

required_facts.statement: Emit a custom analytics event with `await FirebaseAnalytics.instance.logEvent(name: eventName, parameters: parameterMap)`.

Custom parameter names must start with a letter, contain only alphanumeric characters and underscores, and be at most 40 characters; supported parameter values include String and num.

context.concept_name: Investigating common UI slowdown with profile-mode DevTools frame evidence

coverage.learning_objective: Investigate one supplied slow screen in profile mode and identify its common frame bottleneck from evidence.

required_facts.statement: Measure Flutter performance in profile mode on a representative physical device rather than use debug-mode timing as production performance evidence.
Run the application with `flutter run --profile`, open the DevTools Performance view, and record the target interaction.
Each frame includes UI-thread work that builds the layer tree and raster-thread work that rasterizes it.
At 60 Hz, a frame taking more than roughly 16 ms misses the frame budget; at 120 Hz, the budget is roughly 8 ms.
In the Performance view, select a slow frame and compare its UI and raster timings to identify which stage exceeded the budget.
Use frame analysis and timeline events to identify the expensive operation before changing code.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied scrolling interaction feels slow, but debug timing is not production performance evidence. Measure in profile mode on a representative physical device and inspect the slow frame before deciding which code to change.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Measure Flutter performance in profile mode on a representative physical device rather than use debug-mode timing as production performance evidence. Run the application with `flutter run --profile`, open the DevTools Performance view, and record the target interaction. Each frame includes UI-thread work that builds the layer tree and raster-thread work that rasterizes it. At 60 Hz, a frame taking more than roughly 16 ms misses the frame budget; at 120 Hz, the budget is roughly 8 ms. In the Performance view, select a slow frame and compare its UI and raster timings to identify which stage exceeded the budget. Use frame analysis and timeline events to identify the expensive operation before changing code.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The frame comparison needs an applicable refresh-rate budget and two work-stage observations. UI-thread work builds the layer tree, while raster-thread work rasterizes it. A roughly 16 ms frame budget corresponds to 60 Hz and a roughly 8 ms budget to 120 Hz. Compare the selected frame's stage timings with the relevant budget, then use timeline events to locate expensive work. Keep measurement in profile mode on the representative physical device so the evidence is not debug timing mislabeled as production behavior. Recording the supplied interaction before changing code makes the proposed investigation follow observed work rather than a generic guess.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Run `flutter run --profile`, open DevTools Performance, and record the target interaction. Select a slow frame and compare its UI-thread and raster-thread timings. UI work builds the layer tree; raster work rasterizes it. At 60 Hz the frame budget is roughly 16 ms, while at 120 Hz it is roughly 8 ms. Use the frame analysis and timeline events to identify the expensive operation instead of assuming every slow frame is caused by the same UI code.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A debug-mode duration does not establish production performance. Also, a 16 ms budget is not appropriate for every refresh rate, and total slowness does not by itself identify whether UI or raster work exceeded the applicable budget.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the device, interaction, and measurement mode explicit. Compare the selected frame with the target's approximate budget, then follow timeline evidence to the expensive work. Record the observation before making a code change. Keep advanced performance techniques outside this bounded first-frame investigation.

context.concept_name: Identifying unnecessary widget rebuilds

coverage.learning_objective: Trace one unrelated subtree rebuild to its causing state dependency using supplied instrumentation.

required_facts.statement: Enable Track Widget Builds in DevTools Performance tracing to show named widget build events in the timeline.
Trigger the state change once and correlate the resulting subtree build events with the instrumented model notifications or setState call.
A setState call invalidates its State's subtree, while a provider watch subscribes its calling widget to model changes; trace which dependency or ancestor invalidation reaches the unrelated subtree.
Compare the values actually rendered by the rebuilt subtree with the changed state to identify a rebuild caused by an overly broad dependency rather than a relevant visible-data change.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied state change rebuilds a UI section whose displayed values did not change. Investigate the dependency or ancestor invalidation that reached it before calling every rebuild unnecessary. The trace should connect a specific action with specific build events.

teaching_blocks.content: Enable Track Widget Builds in DevTools Performance tracing to show named widget build events in the timeline. A setState call invalidates its State's subtree, while a provider watch subscribes its calling widget to model changes; trace which dependency or ancestor invalidation reaches the unrelated subtree. Compare the values actually rendered by the rebuilt subtree with the changed state to identify a rebuild caused by an overly broad dependency rather than a relevant visible-data change.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Link cause and observed work rather than counting builds without context. One state change has its instrumented notification or setState evidence; Track Widget Builds shows named build events. Trace the watch dependency or ancestor invalidation connecting that change to the rebuilt section. Then compare what the section actually renders with what changed. If its rendered values are unrelated to that change, the trace identifies overly broad dependency work under the supplied example. media.group_title: Reducing unchanged-subtree work with const

segments.label: How const widget identity can reduce redundant updates
segments.summary: Consider a counter screen with an unchanged title and a number that changes after a button press. Making the title's widget configuration const allows Dart to reuse the same constant object. When Flutter receives that identical object during a parent update, it can skip the normal update of the corresponding child element, potentially saving work across an unchanged subtree. This does not prevent the parent from rebuilding or cache the screen as an image. The changing number cannot be const, and layout constraints or inherited dependencies can still cause work. Moving state closer to changing widgets and splitting large widget trees are also suggested. Compare rebuild activity and frame times in DevTools before and after a change: const alone does not guarantee fewer repaints or improved frame rates.

context.concept_name: Identifying and resolving resource-lifetime leaks

coverage.learning_objective: Use supplied retention or subscription-count evidence across repeated route visits to identify one leaking owner and verify that a localized correction stops accumulation.

required_facts.statement: An object remains reachable, and cannot be collected, while a path of references from a root retains it.
Record the baseline retained-instance or active-subscription count, repeat route entry and exit, and compare snapshots or counts for persistent accumulation after the owner exits.
Inspect a retained instance's retaining path to find the owner or callback reference keeping it reachable.
Dispose owned disposable resources and cancel owned subscriptions when their lifetime ends, then repeat the same route visits to verify the retained resource count returns to baseline.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Repeated visits to a supplied route appear to leave resources behind. An object cannot be collected while a reference path from a root keeps it reachable. Look for persistent accumulation after owner exit, then inspect the retaining path that explains it.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: An object remains reachable, and cannot be collected, while a path of references from a root retains it. Record the baseline retained-instance or active-subscription count, repeat route entry and exit, and compare snapshots or counts for persistent accumulation after the owner exits. Inspect a retained instance's retaining path to find the owner or callback reference keeping it reachable. Dispose owned disposable resources and cancel owned subscriptions when their lifetime ends, then repeat the same route visits to verify the retained resource count returns to baseline.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Use reachability to explain the retained instance, not just a rising number. The retaining path shows which root-linked owner or callback reference still reaches the object. Baseline and repeated route-exit counts show persistent accumulation for the supplied resource; cleanup addresses the owning lifetime. Repeat the same route visits after disposing or canceling that owned resource and compare with the same baseline. This keeps diagnosis and verification connected. Leaving a route is an event in the journey, while becoming unreachable is a reference relationship; the retaining path explains why those are not automatically the same outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Record the baseline retained-instance or active-subscription count. Repeat the supplied route entry and exit and compare snapshots or counts after the owner exits. For a retained instance, inspect the retaining path to find the owner or callback reference keeping it reachable. Dispose owned disposable resources and cancel owned subscriptions at lifetime end, then repeat the same visits. The expected verification is that the retained resource count returns to baseline under the supplied measurement.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Leaving a route does not prove every object associated with it became unreachable. A remaining root-to-object reference path prevents collection. Also, an isolated count without a baseline and repeated-visit comparison is not the stated accumulation test.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the resource type, baseline, repeated visits, and post-exit measurements consistent before and after the fix. context.concept_name: Checking current platform target and store requirements before release

coverage.learning_objective: Check one release candidate against supplied dated authoritative platform requirements and identify unmet items.

required_facts.statement: Check the release against the authoritative policy effective on its intended submission date, including the target platform and whether it is a new app, update, or existing-app availability check.

Google Play target-API requirements distinguish new/update submissions from continued availability of existing apps and include platform-specific exceptions and dated deadlines; compare the candidate's target SDK with its applicable row.
Apple publishes dated SDK and toolchain submission requirements; compare the candidate's build SDK and Xcode version with the requirement effective for that upload.

A locally successful build is not evidence that store requirements are satisfied; mark each unmet candidate value against the applicable policy item rather than infer eligibility from the installed toolchain.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied store listing must describe the build that is actually submitted. Text, screenshots, previews, privacy information, and app-content declarations should match its behavior rather than advertise a different feature set.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Keep descriptions, screenshots, previews, and privacy information accurate to the submitted application's actual behavior. context.concept_name: Completing privacy disclosures for application data and permissions

coverage.learning_objective: Complete one supplied disclosure checklist so it matches actual app data and permission behavior.

required_facts.statement: Publish an accessible privacy policy describing collected data, its uses, third-party sharing, retention, deletion, and consent withdrawal.
Inventory data collected or shared by the application and its third-party SDKs rather than report only collection written directly in application code.
Map that actual inventory to the Google Play Data safety declarations, including the relevant collection, sharing, security, and deletion information.
Check privacy declarations against the shipped permission and telemetry behavior and update them when the implementation changes.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied app and its third-party SDKs collect or share data. Store disclosures must describe that actual inventory, not only the collection statements the learner wrote directly. A privacy policy and Data safety declarations should stay aligned with the shipped behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Publish an accessible privacy policy describing collected data, its uses, third-party sharing, retention, deletion, and consent withdrawal. Inventory data collected or shared by the application and its third-party SDKs rather than report only collection written directly in application code. Map that actual inventory to the Google Play Data safety declarations, including the relevant collection, sharing, security, and deletion information. Check privacy declarations against the shipped permission and telemetry behavior and update them when the implementation changes.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Map actual behavior into disclosures rather than mapping desired disclosures back into a fictional build. Include collection and sharing performed by third-party SDKs as well as application code. The policy covers the stated uses, sharing, retention, deletion, and consent withdrawal, while Data safety uses the inventory for its relevant collection/sharing/security/deletion declarations. Compare permission and telemetry implementation with those declarations, especially after a change. The exercise asks for fidelity to the shipped behavior, not new legal advice or invented SDK practices. Keep each supplied inventory item traceable to the applicable disclosure instead of assuming SDK data is outside the application's report.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Inventory application and SDK data collection/sharing. Publish an accessible policy covering collected data, uses, third-party sharing, retention, deletion, and consent withdrawal. Map the real inventory to Google Play Data safety declarations, including relevant collection, sharing, security, and deletion information. Check those declarations against actual permission and telemetry behavior. When implementation changes, update the disclosures rather than retaining a checklist that described an older build.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: An SDK's collection is not excluded simply because application code did not perform it directly. Also, filling out a disclosure form once is not proof it still describes a changed implementation. The inventory and shipped behavior are the grounding inputs.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Use a supplied data-flow inventory and release behavior to compare each applicable disclosure item. Identify discrepancies without inventing legal conclusions or additional data practices. Check policy accessibility and the stated coverage topics, then keep declarations synchronized with the implementation being submitted.

video_need.reason: An inventory-to-disclosure mapping is best taught as a focused checklist, not a store UI tour.

context.concept_name: Preparing review access and verifying release main flows

coverage.learning_objective: Verify one release main flow and supplied reviewer access and identify any blocking failure.

required_facts.statement: Review the release as an actual user-facing application and resolve crashes, bugs, broken links, and incomplete behavior before submission.
Test its release build on the intended supported targets and verify that backend services required by the journey are live and accessible.
Provide working review access, such as a demo account or supported demo mode, for account-gated functionality.
On Google Play, resolve errors reported in the release review summary before publishing; warnings should also be addressed where possible.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied release journey must work for users and reviewers. Review readiness checks the real release build, required services, and access to gated functionality; successful local development is not the complete submission check.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Review the release as an actual user-facing application and resolve crashes, bugs, broken links, and incomplete behavior before submission. Test its release build on the intended supported targets and verify that backend services required by the journey are live and accessible. Provide working review access, such as a demo account or supported demo mode, for account-gated functionality. On Google Play, resolve errors reported in the release review summary before publishing; warnings should also be addressed where possible.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Use the same release journey for the user-facing check and the reviewer-access check. The release build should work on its intended targets with live accessible backend services, and the reviewer should have working access to account-gated functionality. Then inspect Play's release review summary. Errors are resolved before publishing; warnings are addressed where possible, preserving that qualification. A successful startup, a nominal demo account, and an uploaded build are separate observations that do not replace completing the main flow. Record a concrete blocking failure when one exists rather than treating the presence of release artifacts as review readiness.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Review the application as a user-facing release and resolve crashes, bugs, broken links, and incomplete behavior. Test the release build on intended supported targets and verify backend services needed by the journey are live and accessible. Provide working review access, such as the supplied demo account or supported demo mode, for account-gated functionality. On Google Play, resolve release-review-summary errors before publishing and address warnings where possible.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A working app launch does not prove its main journey or reviewer access works. Also, a gated feature cannot be meaningfully reviewed through an unusable demo account. Errors must be resolved, while the guidance for warnings is to address them where possible.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Follow the supplied main flow in the release build on its intended targets. Check the live-service dependency and working review access separately, then compare the Play review summary with the remaining issues. Preserve the distinction between errors and warnings rather than upgrading every warning into an absolute publishing rule.

context.concept_name: Following Google Play and Apple submission checklists with supplied accounts

coverage.learning_objective: Follow one supplied submission workflow and identify its next valid step and review state.

required_facts.statement: Complete the release's required build, listing, app-content declarations, and release notes, then resolve blocking errors in the store review summary before submitting.
Google Play Changes not yet sent for review means changes exist but have not been submitted; send those changes for review through Publishing overview rather than assume upload submitted them.
In review means the store is reviewing the update, not that it has already been published.
For App rejected or Update rejected, read the policy issue, correct it and resubmit, or use the supported appeal process.
Choose the intended testing or production audience and verify the published status and availability; publication timing can be controlled through managed publishing on Google Play.
Uploading an iOS build to App Store Connect first starts build processing; wait for processing to finish before selecting the build for its version and submission workflow.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied store upload is part of submission, not necessarily the act that sends a release for review or publishes it. Track the store's state and next valid action so an uploaded build is not mistaken for an available release.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Complete the release's required build, listing, app-content declarations, and release notes, then resolve blocking errors in the store review summary before submitting. Google Play Changes not yet sent for review means changes exist but have not been submitted; send those changes for review through Publishing overview rather than assume upload submitted them. In review means the store is reviewing the update, not that it has already been published. For App rejected or Update rejected, read the policy issue, correct it and resubmit, or use the supported appeal process. Choose the intended testing or production audience and verify the published status and availability; publication timing can be controlled through managed publishing on Google Play. Uploading an iOS build to App Store Connect first starts build processing; wait for processing to finish before selecting the build for its version and submission workflow.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Complete the required build, listing, app-content declarations, and release notes, then resolve blocking review-summary errors. On Google Play, Changes not yet sent for review requires sending the changes through Publishing overview; In review means review is happening, not publication. For App rejected or Update rejected, read and correct the policy issue and resubmit, or use the supported appeal process. Select the intended testing or production audience and verify published status and availability; managed publishing can control timing. On iOS, wait for uploaded-build processing before selecting it for the version/submission workflow.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Upload, review, and publication are distinct states. A rejected update is not an already-published success, and an iOS upload must finish processing before the build-selection step.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the scope focused
teaching_blocks.content: Read the supplied current state and identify its next permitted action without inventing a processing or review duration.

video_need.reason: Store status and next-action walkthroughs clarify upload, processing, review and publication.
